messages.subject: [S] mixed models, lme, nlme
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to fit a mixed-effects model to some length-weight data.  I
started out using the lme() function, defining the relationship based on
the logs of the lengths and weights.  This was my first time using the lme
() function, but with guidance from Pinheiro and Bates (2000) I was able to
figure things out pretty well.  I ended up with a fit like this:

lme(fixed = lnwt ~ I(lnlen - 4), data = jeffg2, random = pdDiag(~ I(lnlen -
4)))

where jeffg2 is Grouped Data: lnwt ~ lnlen | id2/reach/year.  Upon checking
the assumptions, I discovered that the residuals were not normally
distributed (very long tails in the qqnorm() plot).  So, I thought perhaps
I should try to model the nonlinear relationship instead.  I tried this fit

nlme(wt ~ a * len^b, data = jeffg3, fixed = len ~ 1, start=c(4e-6, 3))

where jeffg3 is Grouped Data: wt ~ len | id2/reach/year and the starting
values come from an nls() fit.  I got a never-ending (or so it seemed ... I
didn't actually wait an eternity) series of "Error during wrapup" messages
that could only be stopped by killing the process (escape) or, by killing
the S-PLUS session (sometimes escape wouldn't stop the job).  Thinking this
might have something to do with the size of the problem (jeffg3 has about
45,000 rows and its number of groups is 142 id2, 217 reach %in% id2, and
255 year %in% reach %in% id2), I tried a smaller simpler fit

nlme(wt ~ a * len^b, data = jeffg1, fixed = len ~ 1, start=c(4e-6, 3),
subset=1:200)

where jeffg1 is Grouped Data: wt ~ len | id2.  I got the same "Error during
wrapup" messages.

So, now I have two questions.  (1) What can I do about the non-normal
residuals from the lme() fit?  (2) What can I do to get the nlme() fit to
work?

Thanks in advance for the help.  Reply to me and I'll summarize to the
group.  I'm using S-PLUS 2000 Professional Release 2 for Windows NT.

JVA

messages.subject: [S] glm/discriminant analysis
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-PLUS users:

I am using S-PLUS Linux 5.1 on RedHatLinux.
I would like to run discriminant analysis for the data in which more than 2 
groups should be discriminated. As a reference, I read a relevant section
in "Modern Applied Biostatistical Methods Using S-Plus" by Steve Selvin.
"glm" function is used for discriminant analysis in that book, but it
treats 2 groups.  In an example there, half of data are from Males and the
rest from Females, and the number of sample with each sex is same.
Therefore, each observation is classified into two groups depending on sex,
and each group has originally either "0" or "1", and later "-0.5" or "0.5".
Sex is dependent variable.

(Q1) Does glm function create new dependent variables when glm is applied
to the data, if the new dependent variables were not explicitely created?
Or is this transformation of dependent variables unnecessary?

(Q2) Is lda function supposed to do a same calculation as glm for
discriminant analysis?

I prefer using glm for discriminant analysis and must find a way to
discriminate more than 2 groups.

-Tadashi

On Thu, 15 Jun 2000, Tadashi Sugihara wrote:

> 
> Dear S-PLUS users:
> 
> I am using S-PLUS Linux 5.1 on RedHatLinux.

> rest from Females, and the number of sample with each sex is same.
> Therefore, each observation is classified into two groups depending on sex,
> and each group has originally either "0" or "1", and later "-0.5" or "0.5".
> Sex is dependent variable.
> 
> (Q1) Does glm function create new dependent variables when glm is applied
> to the data, if the new dependent variables were not explicitely created?
> Or is this transformation of dependent variables unnecessary?

glm with family=binary does logistic discrimination.  You can do LDA for
two groups via lm, but that is not what I recall Selvin is doing.

> (Q2) Is lda function supposed to do a same calculation as glm for
> discriminant analysis?

Is that Professor Ripley's lda function in the MASS library?
If so, no, it actually does discriminant analysis.

> I prefer using glm for discriminant analysis and must find a way to
> discriminate more than 2 groups.

Well, I don't know why you prefer glm to my lda, but if you like
harder-to-use functions ....

My function multinom in library nnet will do logistic discrimination with
more than two groups.  There are worked examples in Venables & Ripley MASS
3rd edition.  Although Selvin's book has a similar title and date, it
was written for a _much_ older version of S-PLUS (3.2, it seems from the
internal evidence) and so does not make use of the extensions written
(mainly by me) in the last five years.

messages.subject: [S] Responses to Post on MLEs for Censored Data
messages.subject_clean: [S] Responses to Post on MLEs for Censored Data
messages.body_plain:
On 6-13-00 I submitted the following post to snews:

> Is anyone aware of Splus functions available to estimate the mean and
> variance parameters of data that
> is normally distributed with some of the observations being censored?
>

First, a big THANKS is in order for all the helpful responses (listed below)
I received. 

I ended up using the functions survreg and Surv, and they worked fine. I 
understand that function censorReg would also do the trick, but apparently
it isn't available on Version 3.4 for a Sun SPARC.

Thanks again,

Jon Binkley
The Aerospace Corp.

>>From Charles Berry

Check the archive. I think this question got asked before. I think the
answer is to use survreg() from the Terneau's survival5 package.

>>From Dennis Murphy,

If you're going to be doing a lot of reliability data analysis, I'd
suggest using the SLIDA software developed by Bill Meeker and Luis
Escobar, which is available only on the PC platform and accompanies their
book. It can be found at
  http://www.public.iastate.edu/~stat533/slida.html
It comes with a users manual, which can be downloaded from the above
page.

>>From Luciano Molinari

Under S+2000 functions survReg and censorReg (Guide to Statistics, Vol.2,
Ch. 11 and 12) do this and more.

>>From Fernando TUSELL

The book "Analysis of Incomplete multivariate Data" by J.L.Schafer
  refers to S-Plus software in his page

    http://www.stat.psu.edu/~jls

  I have not used this, but the port of his package "norm" to R (by
  Alvaro Novo) and it does what you mention to my entire satisfaction.

  The R package, in case yo use R, can be downloaded from CRAN.

  Hope this helps.

>>From  Frank Lawrence

I would be interested in any responses you receive to your post.

>>From  Chuck

Bill Meeker has a suite of S-Plus routines, with a GUI, that do this job
very nicely.  You can get the SLIDA routines (Splus Functions for Life Data
Analysis) from his website.  They're self-extracting and installation is
easy.

http://www.public.iastate.edu/~stat533/slida.html

>>From Rob Leduc

I am studying linear regression (normal errors) with a left
censored response for my Master's.  I've written a routine to
get the MLE in Splus using nlminb.  If you gave my routine the
flat model, it would estimate the mean and variance.  But I don't
do right censoring.  It also computes jackknife standard errors
for these estimates.

I'm happy to share my code with you, although I would have to
clean it up a little for it to be useable by someone besides me.

I would be interested in hearing what others tell you.

>>From Steven McKinney

I used censorReg() extensively a few months back on an environmental
study looking at measured PCB levels, with left-censored
observations due to inability of test procedures to accurately
measure small levels of PCBs.  With censorReg() and survreg()
we were able to implement Lumley and Heagerty's most recent methods
(JASA March 2000) to take account of spatial variability.  The
availability of censorReg() and survreg() saved us months of
programming.

You can e-mail me at
kilroy2718 at sprynet.com
if you need further help or example code.

(I was not working for MathSoft at the time and this opinion
is mine and does not reflect MathSoft etc. etc.)

>>From Catherine

The locfit library (http://cm.bell-labs.com/stat/project/locfit/) can
do that (in particular, the locfit.censor() function). It's designed
for regression models, but can be coerced into just a mean
and variance.

# create a censord normal sample.
> yunob <- rnorm(100)        # the real value of y
> ycens <- rnorm(100)        # censoring variable
> y <- pmin(yunob,ycens)     # observed y
> cens <- (ycens<yunob)      # T (or 1) for censored observations
> x <- seq(0,1,length=100)   # dummy x variable

# compute the fit
> fit <- locfit.censor(x,y,cens,ev="xbar",deg=0,alpha=c(0,100),kern="rect")

The last four arguments coerce it to produce a mean, rather than regression.
It returns a locfit object - to just get the mean
and variance, change the last line of locfit.censor to
return(list(mean=fh, var=sigma*sigma)).

The algorithm is iterative, similar to Schmee and Hahn (1979
technometrics, 417-434). But their variance estimate (and hence
mean) isn't consistent; in locfit the variance estimate is
df-adjusted maximum likelihood.

messages.subject: Fw: [S] Locfit 'bands' won't change colour
messages.body_plain:
I post a working solution:
>From: Catherine Loader <catherine at research.bell-labs.com>
>
>par(col=2) before the second call will work.

Sadly, this just colours the bands, not the regression line!
The solution is, then, par(col=2) before the second call AND col=2 in the
plot statement.
It works!

> I guess you're working in 1-d; the actual plot() and lines() calls
> are in the function plot.locfit.1d(), but it the col argument isn't
> always passed on. Changing (in plot.lcofit.1d)
>
>   if(length(x at se.fit) > 0) {
>     lines(xev[ord], cup, lty = 2)
>     lines(xev[ord], clo, lty = 2)
>  }
>
>to
>
>  if(length(x at se.fit) > 0) {
>    lines(xev[ord], cup, lty = 2, col=col)
>    lines(xev[ord], clo, lty = 2, col=col)
>  }
>
>should also work.
>
>--C.

(NB. I haven't tried the second suggestion, as the first one (modified as
above) works).
Stuart

messages.subject: Re: [S] multivariate time series
messages.body_plain:
There is now a revised version of my DSE library for multivariate time
series available at <www.bank-banque-canada.ca/pgilbert>. The library
works with R and some versions of Splus (see  below). It handles
multivariate ARMA and state space models as well as providing a "classes
and methods" structure for implementing other models and studying
estimation techniques.

There is a user's guide in pdf and ps formats available at the web site.
It is reasonably up to date. There is also a fairly extensive HTML help
facility, but much of the help is in need of revision. (Comments are
always appreciated.)

I use and test the library with Splus 3.3 on Solaris and R on Solaris
and Linux. I believe it should work with Splus 3.4. The library uses
classes and methods extensively and does not yet work with Splus 5.x.
The installation requires compiling fortran or an equivalent C version
of some code. This is typically not a problem on other versions of Unix,
but seems sometimes to be a problem for Windows users.

Paul Gilbert

messages.subject: [S] summary on how to find records which do not appear in both of the dataframes?
messages.subject_clean: [S] summary on how to find records which do not appear in both of the dataframes?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Tim Hesterberg, Winnie Lamber, Bill Dunlap and Robert Garrett 
for
their prompt and helpful replies.  There are several ways to achieve what I
need:

(1) When both dataframe A and B has a different field (or just manually add
a unique field to each dataframe for this particular task), e.g.., "uniqueA"
for dataframe A and "uniqueB" for dataframe B, we can use the combined
wisdom of Winnie Lamber and Robert Garrett
        (a) merge datafram A and dataframe B including all records in both
dataframes
                AB <- merge(A,B,all=T)
        (b) use is.na to extract the records which is in only one of the 
dataframe
                UniqueRecords <- AB[is.na(AB$uniqueA) | is.na(AB$UniqueB),]

(2) Bill Dunlap suggests a universal solution:

        One way to convert your data frame into a character vector is with
        f <- function(dataFrame)
                 do.call("paste", c(lapply(dataFrame, function(x)as.vector(x)),
                        list(sep="\001")))

Putting this together a function, g, that returns the rows of A not in B
and the rows of B not in A would be:

        g <- function(A,B) {
                charA<-f(A)
                charB<-f(B)
                rbind(A[which(is.na(match(charA,charB))),],
                        B[which(is.na(match(charB,charA))),])
        }

(3) When the row names in dataframe A and dataframe B match, Tim Hesterburg
suggests:

        rbind(A[!is.element(row.names(A), row.names(B)),],
        B[!is.element(row.names(B), row.names(A)),])

        Thanks for all the helps again.  Hope everybody has a good weekend!

---Sharon

messages.subject: [S] summary - setting the colours in a levelplot
messages.subject_clean: [S] summary - setting the colours in a levelplot
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I recently asked

> Can someone tell me how to set the colours in a levelplot please?
> I would like the colours to go from light blue to dark blue
> with 'white' or preferably 'transparent' as the background colour.

I received several replies.
Most solutions reflect my overall impression that setting
a color scheme is not intuitive nor particularly easy.

Firstly, most people suggested gui or graphsheet commands 
rather than using arguements to the levelplot command itself,
so it may be necessary to start a new graphsheet each time 
you want to change colours (resetting 'image.color.table').
The relevant help files are under 'graphsheet' and 'postscript'.
e.g. Marcel Baumgartner suggested trellis.device(color=F)
for grey scales.

On Unix, Patrick Connolly suggested specifying your
own colour matrix and getting Trellis to use that.

Andy Liaw suggested looking in the help file for graphsheet
to get definitions for color.scheme, image.color.scheme 
and color.table

Anne E. York offered a useful function to see what the 
colors are on the current graphics device.

The following solution is for Windows versions of SPlus.
You can change the colors for the level plot in Splus 2000 using
the  options - color schemes - image colors.
Two small things that I learned from experimentation are that 
'colour table' (under the 'edit colours' button) 
contains a 'custom colors' table that should be filled in 
from the top row to bottom row 
rather than from left to right along one row.
Secondly, the sum of the column of numbers in the
'# of shades' argument should sum to 100 otherwise
the specified color scheme seems to cycle over.
e.g. if you choose '# of colours' = 4 then try
'# of shades' = 33,33,33.

Staying within the levelplot command,
my subjective choice of dark to light blue is

x <- data.frame(expand.grid(row = 1:8 , 
   col = 1:12 ), level = sample(1:100, 96, T))
x$level[ sample(1:96, 10) ] <- NA
levelplot(level ~ row * col , data = x,
  col.regions = seq(20, 100, length = 100) )
rm(x)

and this looks not unreasonable when printed on paper.

A copy of all the replies is available on request.

Thanks to Andy Liaw, Jim Herndon, Anne E. York,
Megan Pledger, Nick Ellis, Marcel Baumgartner
and Patrick Connolly.

Regards,

John.

John Gavin

messages.subject_clean: [S] New S-Plus functions for Multiple Imputation: MICE
messages.body_plain:
New S-Plus functions for Multiple Imputation: MICE

Multiple Imputation is the method of choice for
complex incomplete data problems. We have developed
new S-Plus functions to perform all steps of
a full Multiple Imputation analysis: Generation
of imputations, repeated analyses on the imputation
data and pooling of the results. Generation of the
imputations is based on Gibbs sampling.

All functions together form the library MICE, which stands for Multivariate
Imputation by Chained Equations.
This library (version 1.0) and a user manual can be obtained from our
website:
http://www.multiple-imputation.com.

The library runs (and is tested) under S-Plus V4.5

Several of you emailed me directly with advice on how to handle NA's in and
IF statement.  Most of the respondents said to use the is.na function, and
other suggestions included using other *.na functions.  Thanks to all who
responded - you know who you are.

(Sharon: did this help?)

Win Lambert

Sharon,

I'm new to this S-PLUS thing, so you may get better advice from someone
else.  But, if you use merge and set all = T, all records will be merged
into the new data frame and the rows that aren't similar will have NA's in
them.  Now, if you can figure out a way to extract the rows that have NA's
in them, you'll have the records that appear in one dataframe, but not the
other - which is what I assume you want.  The problem is extracting those
rows and putting them in another dataframe.  The "IF" statement does not
accept NA's, which is causing me a headache, but I digress.  Can anyone help
Sharon with the second step so she can get what she needs?

Win

messages.subject: [S] Follow up on Extracting non-NULL elements of a list
messages.subject_clean: [S] Follow up on Extracting non-NULL elements of a list
messages.body_plain:
In April there was a thread on extracting non-NULL elements of a list.
Bill Venables had suggested
     for(i in length(ttt):1) ttt[[i]] <- ttt[[i]]
but latter said working backwards wasn't necessary.  I have been utilyzing this
(thanks) and found working backwards is indeed necessary when there are adjacent
NULL elements.

For example:
> ttt <- list(a1 = NULL, a2 = NULL, a3 = NULL, a4 = 1:3, a5 = NULL, a6 = NULL,
   a7 = 1:3)
> for(i in 1:length(ttt))  ttt[[i]] <- ttt[[i]]
> ttt
$a2:
NULL

$a4:
[1] 1 2 3

$a6:
NULL

$a7:
[1] 1 2 3
(a2 and a6  never get evaluated)

Working backwards gives the correct output:
> ttt <- list(a1 = NULL, a2 = NULL, a3 = NULL, a4 = 1:3, a5 = NULL, a6 = NULL,
   a7 = 1:3)
> for(i in length(ttt):1)
   ttt[[i]] <- ttt[[i]]
> ttt
$a4:
[1] 1 2 3

$a7:
[1] 1 2 3

KJJ

messages.subject: [S] Weird polygon() bug?
messages.body_plain:
Hi. I'm experiencing some weird behavior with the polygon() function and I
wonder if anyone else is, too. I'm using S-Plus 2000 (release 1) on NT 4.0.

The function below calls polygon() twice times to produce two square blocks.
Each box has its own "angle" for hatching. The call to polygon() is inside a
for() loop.

When I run the function, only one of the two blocks actually gets shaded.
There's also some stray shading that's in the upper right of the graph, not
in either block. However, if I insert a call to "browser" inside the loop,
and hit 0 ("continue") each time, I get the picture that I've asked for. Is
this weird? Can anyone duplicate this behavior under Windows?

I did not see this problem on a motif device while running S-Plus 3.4
release 1 for Sparc, SUN OS 4.1.3. 

Thanks,
Sam Buttrey

Here's the function:

> graph.test.2
function()
{
#
# Polygon bug(?) example. Draw two bars with a different angles
#
# Set up values for angle; fix density at 12
#
        angle <- c(45, 90)
        density <- 12   #
#
# Draw empty plot. Add axis.
#
        plot(c(0.5, 4.5), c(0, 1), type = "n", xlab = "X", ylab = "Y", main
                 = "Bad Graph", axes = F)
        axis(1, at = 1:4, labels = paste(1:4))  #
#
# Use polygon() to draw a rectangle connecting the points (i, y.lower), 
# (i, y.upper),  (i + .3, y.upper), and (i + .3, y.lower); shade it in.
# 
        y.upper <- 0.25
        y.lower <- 0.125        #
        for(i in 1:2) {
                x.right <- i + 0.3
                polygon(c(i, i, x.right, x.right, i), c(y.lower, y.upper, 
                        y.upper, y.lower, y.lower), col = 1, density = 
                        density, angle = angle[i])      #
        }
        return(NULL)    #
}

messages.subject: [S] Why is "assign" needed in functions?
messages.body_plain:
I find the "assign" statement to be confusing, or perhaps I'm confused by
scoping rules of S.  Consider this simple example:

F_function(dat){
  assign("dat",dat,1)
  dat.aov_aov(y~x,data=dat,qr=T)
  assign("dat.aov",dat.aov,1)
  model.tables(dat.aov)
}

Coming from a Fortran / C++ background, this use of "assign" strikes me as
(1) unnecessary (2) confusing.

My questions:

(1) Why is "assign" needed inside functions?  Is it possible to write
functions without using "assign"?

(2) (More philosophical)  The default behavior of S-plus with regards to
un-assigned objects has caused me countless errors and much swearing.  I
would think that it would be desirable to have objects which are local to a
function be visible to other sub-functions by passing them as arguments to
the sub-functions.  Do people really find the current method of using
"assign" desirable?  I should jolly well think not, so perhaps I'm missing
the boat on some point.

Kevin Wright, Pioneer Hi-Bred Int'l, x4054.

messages.subject: Re: [S] Why is "assign" needed in functions?
messages.body_plain:
I agree that the scoping rules in S are not very natural, but one
can learn to live with them.  The real problem is that the modeling 
functions (aov, lm, glm, gam, etc) are designed as though they will 
always be run from the top-level command line.  Using them inside
functions, and then trying to work with the objects they create,
almost always causes headaches and ugly kludges like
those calls to assign().  For a language that derives much of its 
power from the ease of creating new functions, this is a major
design flaw.  Two years ago there was some discussion in this list
about fixing this (including posts from a MathSoft employee), but 
nothing seems to have happened.

Rich Raubertas
rfr at bst.rochester.edu

This is not exactly unknown, and changing the scope rules of S would

(1) Be a major upheaveal
(2) Break a lot of carefully written code
(3) Whatever they were changed to, introduce further anomalies.

In short, it is not going to happen any time soon.

I don't think the quoted statements are quite fair. I believe those
functions were written in the full knowledge by their authors of the
implications.  Whatever the scope rules are, programmers will need to have
them at their fingertips.  Once you do, having to assign to frame 1 is
surprisingly rare, and you know what to do.  The problem is usually
programmers not using the data= arguments, or not evaluating expressions
in the right frames.

S programming is not an altogether trivial task, which is one reason
Bill Venables and I wrote a monograph about it.

Oh, and the R dialect of S has different scope rules and I am not
convinced that does not lead to an equal number of problems, just different
ones.

messages.subject: [S] differences in 'scan'
messages.body_plain:
I am starting to convert some applications from SPLUS 3.4 to SPLUS 5.1 on a SUN
UNIX machine.  One application reads in a structure with 7M lines with 5 numbers
per line.  These have been setup as integer values and when using the following
scan statement results in a storage mode of 'integer':

scan(file,what=list(a=integer(0),b=integer(0),c=integer(0),d=integer(0),e=integer(0))

The object winds up taking about 140M of space and allocates about twice that
much real memory during the reading process.

Trying the same thing on version 5.1 results in an object twice as large since
the storage mode is 'double'.  I have to follow the 'scan' with a
'lapply(result,as.integer)' to do the conversion.  The problem is that now real
memory is up to 600M just to do the 'scan'.

Is there some functionality that was lost in going to version 5.x?

Here is a sample from version 3.4:

> a.2_scan(,what=0)
1: 1 2 3 4
5:
> a.2
[1] 1 2 3 4
> storage.mode(a.2)
[1] "double"
> a.2_scan(,what=integer(0))
1: 1 2 3 4
5:
> storage.mode(a.2)
[1] "integer"

This works the way I would expect it.  Here is version 5.1:

> a.1_scan(,what=0)
1: 1 2 3 4
5:
> storage.mode(a.1)
[1] "double"
> a.1_scan(,what=integer(0))
1: 1 2 3 4
5:
> storage.mode(a.1)
[1] "double"
>

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
         I have been using the gam() and step.gam() functions in S-Plus 4.5
(Professional release 2) to correlate the abundance of estuarine fishes to
their environment. But there are a couple of quirks, that I am not yet able
to master properly.

1)I am modeling the error distribution as a Poisson distribution, but the
behaviour of the species suggest, that they should be more evenly
distributed than a true Poisson process after accounting for the
environmental conditions. Therefore I would like the gam function to
determine the correct dispersion parameter. According to the book 'Modern
Applied Statistics with S-Plus', this is supposed to work by setting
dispersion=0 in the function. At some point this did work, but I changed
something and I cannot figure out what. Since then gam uses the default
dispersion and no matter what I set it to it will only use dispersion=1. The
code I am currently using is:

full.gam <- gam(Age.class ~ offset(Prop1) + BTYPE + YEAR + MONTH + 
    INLDISMC + SFST.TEM + SFST.SAL + STDEPTH + P.COVER,
        family = poisson, link = log, variance = "mu", dispersion=0)
summary(full.gam)

2)In the step.gam() function I would like to keep the offset term in the
function, whether it contributes to the explained deviance or not. The
samples are collected with different sized gears, but unfortunately the
different gears are employed in different environments. In this case the
differences between the gears are at least partially incorrectly attributed
to differences in the environment. So, I need to keep the term in all
possible models the step.gam() function examines. I have tried to leave it
out of the scope altogether, but this results in it being thrown out. If I
use the scope,:

                                                 "offset(Prop1)" ~ 1 +
offset(Prop1)

the offset is thrown out of the model. If I try to use:

                                                 "offset(Prop1)"~
offset(Prop1)

it gives me a cannot untangle scope error. I tried the keep statement, which
I am not sure will do the right thing, but I tried it anyway:

                                                 ... ,
keep=offset(Prop1),...

 just to come up with the following error message, probably because I am not
using the right syntax. (I cannot find much on the correct syntax in either
the manuals or the S
+ programming books I have)

  Warning in step.gam(full.gam, scope = list(BTYPE =  ~ 1 + BTYPE,      :
looking for function "keep", ignored local non-function
Error in step.gam(full.gam, scope = list(BTYP..: couldn't find function
"keep"
Dumped

3)I have some categorical variables in my model which I am interested in. In
particular a year effect, for which I would like to get the least-squares
mean. In the gam summary, there are of course only n-1 parameters estimated,
since it is only interested in relative effects and the last (or may be the
first) parameter is summed into the intercept, but the situation seems more
complicated than this. From some experiments with artificial datasets I have
gleaned, that the first estimate describes the difference between the first
to categories, but the second estimate describes the difference between the
mean of the first two and the third parameter, the third estimate the
difference between the fourth and the first three etc. This is confirmed by
the section on contratst in several books. But how do I get back to the
effect on the scale of the response, or at least the scale of the additive
predictor equivalent to a least squares mean in a GLM? Is this what the
function contr.sdif() in the MASS library does?

                                                Thanks for comments on any
of these points

                                                        Sven Kupschus (a
converted SAS- Programmer)

messages.subject: [S] Error messages (Summary)
messages.body_plain:
In an email to MathSoft, copied to S-News, I complained that, when reading 
an imperfect ASCII file, S-Plus crashed or gave uninformative error 
messages.  I asked whether this couldn't be improved in future releases of 
S-Plus.

I received replies from three persons.  Ellipses and [edits] are mine:

Kevin Wright said:

> I would agree that the error messages can be cryptic and frustrating and
> that S-Plus crashes far too often.
>
>
>
> It is a concern of mine that S-Plus has fallen into the "more features is
> better" syndrome...
>
>
>
> [We hear] that internal builds of S-Plus 6 do not suffer from a particular
> bug problem. My reaction to that is, "Why are they developing S-Plus 6 so
> soon? Why not have a number of incremental releases that offer greatly
> improved reliability and robustness?"

In another message, Kevin gave several examples of cryptic error messages 
from S-Plus.

David Smith of MathSoft replied:

> No mistakes of your own here -- the fault lies fair and square with
> MathSoft. I know from my own experience that getting data into S-PLUS is
> easy when the files are in perfect shape, but if there's an error you're
> usually on your own. And since data are generally a bit messy this can be
> pretty frustrating.
>
>
>
> The enhancement request is most definitely noted for S-PLUS 6.

Last but certainly not least, Nicole DePriest pointed out that 
count.fields() can be used to find the offending line in the ASCII 
file.  Clearly, there is a diagnostic available that I had overlooked.

I thank all responders and I do hope that MathSoft will be able to improve 
the situation.  Though I occasionally use and enjoy the GUI features of 
S-Plus, I agree that stability and good error handling are more important 
than a multiplicity of features.  In using S-Plus, I have identified bugs 
or misfeatures that I'd hope to have fixed before a next major release, and 
other areas of apparent development emphasis (OLE, DDE, and such) that, 
being platform-specific, configuration-dependent, and of dubious endurance 
and minimal robustness (not MathSoft's fault!), I know that I will never 
use.  However, my taste in software is far from universal.

I would hope that MathSoft could look not just at reading ASCII files, but 
at error messages in S-Plus in general.  Many of the ones I have received 
have little apparent connection to the offending code.  If one is deeply 
familiar with S architecture, the messages might not be so baffling.  But I 
doubt most users are at that level.  This situation increases my debugging 
time by at least 50%.

Thanks again to those who responded and to MathSoft for any attempt to 
improve the situation.

--
Michael Prager      <Mike.Prager at noaa.gov>
NOAA Beaufort Laboratory
Beaufort, North Carolina  28516  USA

messages.subject: Re: [S] Why is "assign" needed in functions?
messages.body_plain:
Actually my objection is not to the scoping rules, and I agree
that it is out of the question to change them at this point.  I'm
sorry my post was not clear on this.  My complaint is about 
the modeling functions (and apparently Trellis functions as 
well).  I think they could be improved without touching the scoping
rules.  

The problem is that objects created by the modeling functions
are not self-contained.  If I create an object using data.frame(), 
all the built-in methods work with that object whether or not
I am at the command line; no use of assign() is ever needed.  I do 
not see any logical reason why an object produced by gam() should
behave any differently.  I assume the designers felt that making
gam() objects self-contained would take up too much space, but that
seems a decision that should be left to users.  A possible 
solution is (1) Add a 'keep.args' argument to the modeling functions.
keep.args=T would cause all[*] of the (evaluated) arguments to be 
included as part of the returned object.  Making the default 
keep.args=F would ensure backward compatibility. (2) Change the 
associated method functions (plot, predict, etc) to first check 
the object itself for any needed information, before searching 
through frames.  I don't think this would break any existing
code.

[*] Note that keeping just the 'data' argument is not enough.  I
often use constructs like

frm <- as.formula(paste(resp.var,"~",paste(covar,collapse="+")))
z <- gam(frm, data=d)
plot(z)

where resp.var and covar are character variables.  This fails 
inside a function because 'frm' is not found by plot.  Similar
situations arise with the 'subset' and 'weights' arguments.

Rich Raubertas
rfr at bst.rochester.edu

> Date: Tue, 20 Jun 2000 22:47:02 +0100 (BST)
> From: Prof Brian D Ripley <ripley at stats.ox.ac.uk>
> 
> On Tue, 20 Jun 2000, Mike Prager wrote:
> 
> > At 6/20/00 at 04:48 PM, Richard Raubertas wrote:
> > 
> > >The real problem is that the modeling
> > >functions (aov, lm, glm, gam, etc) are designed as though they will
> > >always be run from the top-level command line.  Using them inside
> > >functions, and then trying to work with the objects they create,
> > >almost always causes headaches and ugly kludges like
> > >those calls to assign().
> > 
> > As I found out not more than 10 minutes ago, your comments on modeling 
> > functions apply to Trellis graphics functions, as well.
> 
> This is not exactly unknown, and changing the scope rules of S would
> 
> (1) Be a major upheaveal
> (2) Break a lot of carefully written code
> (3) Whatever they were changed to, introduce further anomalies.
> 
> In short, it is not going to happen any time soon.
> 
> I don't think the quoted statements are quite fair. I believe those
> functions were written in the full knowledge by their authors of the
> implications.  Whatever the scope rules are, programmers will need to have
> them at their fingertips.  Once you do, having to assign to frame 1 is
> surprisingly rare, and you know what to do.  The problem is usually
> programmers not using the data= arguments, or not evaluating expressions
> in the right frames.
> 
> S programming is not an altogether trivial task, which is one reason
> Bill Venables and I wrote a monograph about it.
> 
> Oh, and the R dialect of S has different scope rules and I am not
> convinced that does not lead to an equal number of problems, just different
> ones.
>

On Wed, 21 Jun 2000, Sarah Goslee wrote:

> 
> Well, I'm stumped. I've been thinking about this problem for
> quite a while, on and off, and finally decided it was time

> My problem involves the permutation version of the paired
> t-test, which has been published & discussed in a number
> of stats book. For example, the shoe data example in the
> permutation section of V&R:
> 
> attach(shoes)
> d <- B-A
> ttest <- function(x) mean(x)/sqrt(var(x)/length(x))
> n <- 1000
> res <- numeric(x)
> for(i in 1:n) {
>       x <- d*sign(runif(10)-0.5)
>       res[i] <- ttest(x)
> }

> For those not familiar with this example, the basic idea
> is that A and B are groups to be compared. This test
> randomizes the group assignment by switching the sign of
> the difference between A and B.

> The problem is that for a long sequence of random numbers, the
> tendency is to get roughly equal numbers of + and -, so that the
> possible distribution is not well-sampled. The permutations are
> biased towards the middle of the potential distribution.

That's called the central limit theorem, and is a consequence of
well-sampling.

> In 1000 repetitions of the randomization for 10 samples, the
> distribution covers the range of possibilities:
> 
> The number of + values in 1000 reps of d*sign(runif(10)-0.5) is:
> 
> > summary(perm10.sum)
>  Min. 1st Qu. Median  Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 
>     0       4      5 5.036       6   10
> 
> When the same thing is done for a sample size of 100,
> the number of + values in d*sign(runif(100)-0.5) is:
> 
> summary(perm100.sum)
>  Min. 1st Qu. Median  Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 
>    36      47     50 49.92      53   66
> 
> The tails of the permutation distribution are not at all
> well-sampled, it seems to me, and this certainly affects
> the final p-value.

That number is binomial(50, 0.5) distributed.

> pbinom(c(32, 46, 47, 53, 54, 66), 100, 0.5)
[1] 0.0002043886 0.2420592068 0.3086497068 0.7579407932 0.8158991913
[6] 0.9995631401

which looks about right. Values less than 33 or greater than 66 are
implausible in 1000 replicates, and the quartiles are about 46 and 53.

> So.... is this actually a problem? If not, why? If so,

No, because we have theory to which the results conform.

messages.subject: [S] paired difference - permutation test
messages.body_plain:
Well, I'm stumped. I've been thinking about this problem for
quite a while, on and off, and finally decided it was time 
to ask for help.

My problem involves the permutation version of the paired
t-test, which has been published & discussed in a number
of stats book. For example, the shoe data example in the
permutation section of V&R:

attach(shoes)
d <- B-A
ttest <- function(x) mean(x)/sqrt(var(x)/length(x))
n <- 1000
res <- numeric(x)
for(i in 1:n) {
        x <- d*sign(runif(10)-0.5)
        res[i] <- ttest(x)
}

For those not familiar with this example, the basic idea
is that A and B are groups to be compared. This test
randomizes the group assignment by switching the sign of
the difference between A and B.

So far so good- this test works beautifully with the 10-sample
shoe data. It seems to fall apart with larger data sets, though.
The problem is that for a long sequence of random numbers, the
tendency is to get roughly equal numbers of + and -, so that the
possible distribution is not well-sampled. The permutations are
biased towards the middle of the potential distribution.

In 1000 repetitions of the randomization for 10 samples, the
distribution covers the range of possibilities:

The number of + values in 1000 reps of d*sign(runif(10)-0.5) is:

> summary(perm10.sum)
 Min. 1st Qu. Median  Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 
    0       4      5 5.036       6   10

When the same thing is done for a sample size of 100,
the number of + values in d*sign(runif(100)-0.5) is:

summary(perm100.sum)
 Min. 1st Qu. Median  Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 
   36      47     50 49.92      53   66

The tails of the permutation distribution are not at all
well-sampled, it seems to me, and this certainly affects
the final p-value.

So.... is this actually a problem? If not, why? If so,
how do we fix it?

Thank you for the help,
Sarah

-- 
*--*--*--*--*--*--*--*--*--*--*--*--*--*--*

> {

> 
> I know the answer probably lies somewhere in VR3 or VRProg.  I don't have 
> either handy right now, unfortunately.

R has a function is.R() and the definition is (V&R R Complements)

is.R <- function () 
exists("version") && !is.null(vl <- version$language) && vl == "R"

For recentish versions of R, the test

is.R <- function() exists("R.version")

suffices. But (see our Sprog scripts)

if(exists(is.R) && is.R)

is a sufficient test for R.

Testing the version number is useful to distinguish S-PLUS versions
(and the V&R scripts have numerous examples).

V&R use a Perl-based macro-preprocessor for S-PLUS 3.x/4.x/2000/5.1 / R
code, and that is in the on-line material for Sprog (as we tend to call
it).

On Wed, 21 Jun 2000, Sarah Goslee wrote:

>
> Well, I'm stumped. I've been thinking about this problem for
> quite a while, on and off, and finally decided it was time
> to ask for help.
>
> My problem involves the permutation version of the paired
> t-test, which has been published & discussed in a number
> of stats book. For example, the shoe data example in the
> permutation section of V&R:
>
> attach(shoes)
> d <- B-A
> ttest <- function(x) mean(x)/sqrt(var(x)/length(x))
> n <- 1000
> res <- numeric(x)
> for(i in 1:n) {
>          x <- d*sign(runif(10)-0.5)
>          res[i] <- ttest(x)
> }
>
> For those not familiar with this example, the basic idea
> is that A and B are groups to be compared. This test
> randomizes the group assignment by switching the sign of
> the difference between A and B.
>
> So far so good- this test works beautifully with the 10-sample
> shoe data. It seems to fall apart with larger data sets, though.
> The problem is that for a long sequence of random numbers, the
> tendency is to get roughly equal numbers of + and -, so that the
> possible distribution is not well-sampled. The permutations are
> biased towards the middle of the potential distribution.

That's called the central limit theorem, and is a consequence of
well-sampling.

> In 1000 repetitions of the randomization for 10 samples, the
> distribution covers the range of possibilities:
>
> The number of + values in 1000 reps of d*sign(runif(10)-0.5) is:
>
> > summary(perm10.sum)
>  Min. 1st Qu. Median  Mean 3rd Qu. Max.
>     0       4      5 5.036       6   10
>
> When the same thing is done for a sample size of 100,
> the number of + values in d*sign(runif(100)-0.5) is:
>
> summary(perm100.sum)
>  Min. 1st Qu. Median  Mean 3rd Qu. Max.
>    36      47     50 49.92      53   66
>
> The tails of the permutation distribution are not at all
> well-sampled, it seems to me, and this certainly affects
> the final p-value.

That number is binomial(50, 0.5) distributed.

> pbinom(c(32, 46, 47, 53, 54, 66), 100, 0.5)
[1] 0.0002043886 0.2420592068 0.3086497068 0.7579407932 0.8158991913
[6] 0.9995631401

which looks about right. Values less than 33 or greater than 66 are
implausible in 1000 replicates, and the quartiles are about 46 and 53.

> So.... is this actually a problem? If not, why? If so,

No, because we have theory to which the results conform.

messages.subject: Re: [S] paired difference - permutation test
messages.body_plain:
Brian Cade wrote:
>Brian Ripley's interpretation seems correct to me.  So the solution for a
>problem of this size (n = 100) is to make a lot more sample permutations (I
>suggest 10,000 for most analyses) to approximate the 2^100 (a very big
>number) possible permutations under the null.

The appropriate number of random permutations to use for a simulation-based
permutation test depends on the desired accuracy, and how far out in
the tails you want relatively-accurate answers.  If `r' is the number
of replications, `p' is the true p-value, and pHat the simulation-based
estimate, then the relevant standard errors are
        std error of p-hat = sqrt(p * (1-p) / r)
        std error of (p-hat)/p = sqrt((1-p) / (r * p))
Note that these are independent of `n'.

If you do want to use larger numbers of simulations the original code
will be very slow.  This version runs about 450 times faster:

  # d is a vector of length 10 of paired differences
  signed.d <- sign(runif(10 * 1000) - .5) * d
  dim(signed.d) <- c(10, 1000)  # matrix, each replication in one column
  res <- colMeans(signed.d) / sqrt(colVars(signed.d) / length(d))

than the original:

>> ttest <- function(x) mean(x)/sqrt(var(x)/length(x))
>> n <- 1000
>> res <- numeric(n)
>> for(i in 1:n) {
>>          x <- d*sign(runif(10)-0.5)
>>          res[i] <- ttest(x)
>> }

V&R found similar differences in speed between two variations of
code for the exact (non-simulation) version of this same problem.
In general, the best way to make things run quickly in S-PLUS
is to avoid loops.

messages.subject: Re: [S] Transfer between R and S-PLUS
messages.body_plain:
Mike Prager wrote -

....

BDR>>Oh, and the R dialect of S has different scope rules and I am not
>>convinced that does not lead to an equal number of problems, just
>>different ones.

>Interesting observation, and one that seems to imply that the road
>from S to R and back again will be a rocky one for the user.

It depends on what one is doing.  If the use of R and S-PLUS does not
go much beyond writing functions for one's own use, my experience has
been that it is pretty easy to make the transition, in both
directions.  It is necessary to be aware of a few key differences.
Some that occur to me are: 

R's handling of NA is more intuitive; x[x<1] <- y[x<1] is pretty
much a disaster in S-PLUS if x has missing values

the default parameterisation of factors in R uses contrasts with a
baseline level (`treatment' contrasts, not S-PLUS's `helmert'
contrasts which novices rightly find puzzling),

assign(.., frame=1) is often needed in S-PLUS where the structure is
anyway visible in R,

constructs such as I(x^2) are needed in R model formulae where in
S-PLUS one can get away without them.

output structures from R functions may be different from their 
S-PLUS couterparts, and one needs to check.

I have found it fairly easy to move between R and S-PLUS in the
courses that we run for graduate students.  This has turned up
a few instances where a minor S-PLUS functionality that one needs
is missing in R.  Usually it has been easy to add.  My notes
"Data Analysis and Graphics Using R" started in an S-PLUS
incarnation.  It was reasonably easy (and highly educational) to
convert across both the examples and the graphs.

messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 21 Jun 2000, Tim Hesterberg wrote:

> Brian Cade wrote:
> >Brian Ripley's interpretation seems correct to me.  So the solution for a
> >problem of this size (n = 100) is to make a lot more sample permutations (I
> >suggest 10,000 for most analyses) to approximate the 2^100 (a very big
> >number) possible permutations under the null.
> 
> The appropriate number of random permutations to use for a simulation-based
> permutation test depends on the desired accuracy, and how far out in
> the tails you want relatively-accurate answers.  If `r' is the number
> of replications, `p' is the true p-value, and pHat the simulation-based
> estimate, then the relevant standard errors are
>       std error of p-hat = sqrt(p * (1-p) / r)
>       std error of (p-hat)/p = sqrt((1-p) / (r * p))
> Note that these are independent of `n'.

There is nothing in the problem that demands iid simulations. As we
know the distribution of the number N of +'s, we can do conditional
simulation (conditional on N, using abs(differences)) to improve on these
(dramatically in the far tails).

> If you do want to use larger numbers of simulations the original code
> will be very slow.  This version runs about 450 times faster:
> 
>   # d is a vector of length 10 of paired differences
>   signed.d <- sign(runif(10 * 1000) - .5) * d
>   dim(signed.d) <- c(10, 1000)  # matrix, each replication in one column
>   res <- colMeans(signed.d) / sqrt(colVars(signed.d) / length(d))

colMeans and colVars postdate by several years the V&R code, though,
and are not in some currently-used versions of S-PLUS (like 3.4).

> than the original:
> 
> >> ttest <- function(x) mean(x)/sqrt(var(x)/length(x))
> >> n <- 1000
> >> res <- numeric(n)
> >> for(i in 1:n) {
> >>          x <- d*sign(runif(10)-0.5)
> >>          res[i] <- ttest(x)
> >> }
> 
> V&R found similar differences in speed between two variations of
> code for the exact (non-simulation) version of this same problem.
> In general, the best way to make things run quickly in S-PLUS
> is to avoid loops.

Better simulation design will also help.  V&R wanted the whole exact
distribution, for example to compute distances from the approximating
normal.  In larger samples (than 10), theoretical bounds would have
sufficed, too.

messages.subject: Re: [S] weights in glm's
messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 21 Jun 2000, Michael Conklin wrote:

> 
> Dear S experts:
> 
> I am confused by the help file on glm and gam. Is it appropriate to use
> case weights in fitting these models or do the weights refer to
> something else.  I would like to use the functions as part of a mixture
> model but to do so requires the use of case weights. Any help would be
> appreciated.

Weights are part of the definition of a glm family (see any of the texts).
As I understand the term they are `case weights' in that a weight of w
multiplies the log-likelihood contribution by w.  (Well, for known
dispersion parameter, at least.)

For mixture modelling you presumably need fractional cases, but that looks 
OK too.

messages.subject_clean: SUMMARY: [S] system() under Win: how to get a DOS window closed automatically
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Hong Ooi (hong.ooi at maths.anu.edu.au), Brian D. Ripley
(ripley at stats.ox.ac.uk) and Steve Wofsy [scw at io.harvard.edu] who replied on
my question. I attach their responses after the question.

-----Original Message-----

Dear S+ users,
I am going to perform simulations using S+ to prepare data and an external
program running at DOS level for simulation itself. I use the system()
function with multi=F option to run that DOS program. When the program stops
it returns the control to S+, and everything is fine except the MSDOS window
is not closed. If I have to do just 10 runs it is not the problem: I can
close 10 windows manually. However, if I do a lot of silumation (100 or
more) it becomes a real problem. Any suggestions will be appreciated.
I use S+ 4.5 under Win 95/98.
Best regards,
Vladimir

============================================================================
=
Hong Ooi relies:

That's probably more to do with your default .pif settings than with
Splus. Go to the Properties dialog box for your DOS window and make sure
that the "Close on exit" box is checked.

Brian D. Ripley replies:

Set the properties on your DOS program to `Close Window on Exit': the
problem is at that end, not with S-PLUS.

Steve Wofsy replies:

This problem is fixed using dos() and setting the window parameters
correctly to
run in background.  the dos window flashes up on the taskbar, but that's
all.
as in:

print("Create run.bat  to compress the files in c:\\solve\\er2\\temp")
dos("command /C c:\\solve\\comprs.bat")
dos("move /Y c:\\solve\\run.bat c:\\solve\\er2\\temp")

note the use of command /C instead of executing comprs.bat directly.

messages.subject: [S] SUMMARY: weights in glm
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Tim Hesterberg and Brian Ripley for their prompt responses. As
Tim noted, a good way to see how the program works is to try it out with
some known data.  What I wanted to know was if the weights gave results
that were equivalent to repeating each case_i, w_i times in the data.
The following script demonstrates that parameter estimates and parameter
standard errors are identical. The residual deviance is also identical
but the degrees of freedom reported for the residual deviance is based
on the actual N, not the weighted N.  

# example of weighted and unweighted glms
# test data repeats cases 1:50
test.y<-factor(c(rep(rbinom(50,1,.5),2),rbinom(50,1,.5)))
test.x<-c(rep(runif(50),2),runif(50))
# unweighted glm
summary(glm(test.y~test.x,family=binomial),cor=F)
# now weight the first 50 cases by a factor of 2 and then
# eliminate the next 50 cases
test.y2<-test.y[c(1:50,101:150)]
test.x2<-test.x[c(1:50,101:150)]
wts<-rep(c(2,1),c(50,50))
summary(glm(test.y2~test.x2,family=binomial,weights=wts),cor=F)

****************************************

messages.subject: [S] bug in GAM ?
messages.body_plain:
[Apologies if this is already known.]

Possible bug in gam():

 | Version 5.1 Release 1 for Silicon Graphics Irix, IRIX 6.2 : 1999 
 |
 | > df <- data.frame(x=1:10, y=1:10, w=rep(1,10))
 | > gam(y ~ lo(x), family=poisson, weights=w, data=df)
 |
 | Problem in apply(Rsw^2 + 2 * s * resid, 2, sum): 
 |                                dim(X) must have a positive length 
 |
 | > traceback()
 | 5: stop("dim(X) must have a positive length")
 | 4: apply(Rsw^2 + 2 * s * resid, 2, sum)
 | 3: gam.nlchisq(fit$qr, fit$resid, wz, fit$smooth)
 | 2: gam(y ~ lo(x), family = poisson, weights = w, data = df)
 | 1: 
 |
 | > gam(y ~ lo(x), family=poisson, data=df)
 | Call:
 | gam(formula = y ~ lo(x), family = poisson, data = df)
 | 
 | Degrees of Freedom: 10 total; 5.18092 Residual
 | Residual Deviance: 0.03513 
 | 

The expression (Rsw^2 + 2 * s * resid) evaluated in the last line of
gam.nlchisq() turns out to be an n x 1 matrix when gam() is called
without the 'weights' argument, but when this argument is used, 
then (Rsw^2 + 2 * s * resid) is a vector, and dim() yields NULL for vectors.

FIX:  replacing the last line of gam.nlchisq() by
        
        apply(as.matrix(Rsw^2 + 2 * s * resid), 2, sum)

seems to work. 

----
Adrian Baddeley, Mathematics & Statistics, University of Western Australia
                <http://maths.uwa.edu.au/~adrian/>

messages.subject: Re: [S] SUMMARY: weights in glm
messages.body_plain:
Michael Conklin wrote:

>Thanks to Tim Hesterberg and Brian Ripley for their prompt responses. As
>Tim noted, a good way to see how the program works is to try it out with
>some known data.  What I wanted to know was if the weights gave results
>that were equivalent to repeating each case_i, w_i times in the data.
>The following script demonstrates that parameter estimates and parameter
>standard errors are identical. The residual deviance is also identical
>but the degrees of freedom reported for the residual deviance is based
>on the actual N, not the weighted N.  

Below is part of my note to Mike.  The main point is how weights are
interpreted; they do not correspond to repeats, but rather that
the response variable represents <averages> of varying numbers of "real"
cases (when the weights are integer-valued).

============================================================

By "case weights", do you mean that a weight of 2 on an observation
should give results equivalent to repeating the observation twice?

I believe the answer is no.  I haven't looked at glm or gam
in this regard, but I have looked at lm; in that case,
a weight of 2 is equivalent to indicating that the corresponding
y-value is the average of 2 "real" observations with the same
values of x.  This gives equivalent results for estimating
coefficients as the "case weights" model, but standard errors
and other inferences are different.

The following draft documentation relates to lm; it may help
you with glm and gam.  I'd also appreciate if you tell me about any
problems you find with this, or what you learn about glm and gam.
My goal is to have good documentation on the effect of weights in
various modeling functions.

----------------------
The model for lm() in the absence of weights is that
        Y_i = X_i beta + eps_i
where X_i is a 1 by p matrix (the i'th row of the design matrix)
and 
        eps_i ~ N(0, sigma^2)
with sigma^2 unknown.

When weights are present, the model is that
        Y_i = X_i beta + eps_i (as before)
except that
        eps_i ~ N(0, sigma_i^2)
with
        sigma^2_i = sigma^2 / w_i
with sigma^2 unknown.
In contrast, absolute weights correspond to sigma^2 = 1.

This model is appropriate if the i'th observation is the AVERAGE of w_i
"real" observations, each with variance sigma^2.
That is not the same as assuming that the i'th observation represents
a single "real" observation repeated w_i times.
While the regression coefficients are the same, the standard
errors and other inferences are not.  

(continued with examples, that emphasize points consistent with Mike's
nice summary above)

========================================================

| timh at statsci.com     MathSoft, Inc.                  |

Hi folks,
I have a question that I hope is not embarrassingly straightforward. I
would like to determine an exact p-value for a (one variable) multinomial
goodness-of-fit test. The procedure would be as follows. What is given is
a sample size n, a number of categories k, and a set of null probabilities
(p1, ..., pk).

(1) Generate each possible one-dimensional table (n1, ..., nk). That is,
    each possible set of nonnegative integers {n1, ..., nk} s.t. 
    n1 + ... + nk = n.
(2) Calculate the associated multinomial probability of that table.
(3) Calculate the goodness-of-fit test (Peason chi-squared, LR chi-
    squared, etc.).
(4) The tail probability is the sum of the probabilities from (2)
    that come from tables with test statistic (3) at least as large as the
    observed statistic.

My questions come from steps (1) and (2). Is there an easy way to generate
all of the possible tables in (1)? Does anyone have a function that gives
multinomial probabilities given the observed counts and assumed
probability vector?

Thanks for any help.

                 Best,

                 Jeff Simonoff

messages.subject: Re: [S] exact p-value for multinomial goodness-of-fit (fwd)
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks, 
Albyn Jones has also provided answers to my question about exact p-values
for multinomial goodness-of-fit. His function for the multinomial
probability function is very similar to Scott Chasalow's, but his function
to generate all of the possible multinomial tables is remarkable in its
simplicity. One drawback is that the function cannot save the results to a
matrix, but can only print them out. The details are given below.

                      Best,

                      Jeff

My original post:

> 
> Hi folks,
> I have a question that I hope is not embarrassingly straightforward. I
> would like to determine an exact p-value for a (one variable) multinomial
> goodness-of-fit test. The procedure would be as follows. What is given is
> a sample size n, a number of categories k, and a set of null probabilities
> (p1, ..., pk).
> 
> (1) Generate each possible one-dimensional table (n1, ..., nk). That is,
>     each possible set of nonnegative integers {n1, ..., nk} s.t. 
>     n1 + ... + nk = n.
> (2) Calculate the associated multinomial probability of that table.
> (3) Calculate the goodness-of-fit test (Peason chi-squared, LR chi-
>     squared, etc.).
> (4) The tail probability is the sum of the probabilities from (2)
>     that come from tables with test statistic (3) at least as large as the
>     observed statistic.
> 
> My questions come from steps (1) and (2). Is there an easy way to generate
> all of the possible tables in (1)? Does anyone have a function that gives
> multinomial probabilities given the observed counts and assumed
> probability vector?
> 
> Thanks for any help.
> 
>                  Best,
> 
>                  Jeff Simonoff
> 

Hi Jeff

(2) seems easy enough

dmultinom <- function(x,p)
{
if(sum(p) != 1.0) stop ("probabilities must add to 1.0")
if(any(p == 0)) warning("p should have no zero entries")
n <- sum(x)
exp(lgamma(n+1)-sum(lgamma(x+1))+sum(x*log(p)))
}

> dmultinom(c(5,5),c(.5,.5))
[1] 0.2460938

> dbinom(5,10,.5)
[1] 0.2460938
> 

works for this case :-)

for (1) my local computer scientist suggests a recursive algorithm
which I have attempted to code in S:

multenum <- function(k,n,x=numeric()){
# k = number of categories
# n = total count
# x = list of category counts

if(k > 1){
   for(i in 0:n){
multenum(k-1,n-i,c(i,x))
}
}
else print(c(n,x))
return()
}
------------------------------------------------------------------
http://www.reed.edu/~jones    Albyn Jones         jones at reed.edu
Reed College, Portland OR 97202             (503)-771-1112 x7418

messages.body_plain:
Jeff Simonoff reports:
> 
> Hi folks, 
> Albyn Jones has also provided answers to my question about exact p-values
> for multinomial goodness-of-fit. His function for the multinomial
> probability function is very similar to Scott Chasalow's, but his function
> to generate all of the possible multinomial tables is remarkable in its
> simplicity. One drawback is that the function cannot save the results to a
> matrix, but can only print them out. The details are given below.
> 
> 
> for (1) my local computer scientist suggests a recursive algorithm
> which I have attempted to code in S:
> 
> multenum <- function(k,n,x=numeric()){
> # k = number of categories
> # n = total count
> # x = list of category counts
> 
> if(k > 1){
>    for(i in 0:n){
> multenum(k-1,n-i,c(i,x))
> }
> }
> else print(c(n,x))
> return()
> }

It's actually not hard to adapt Albyn's function so that the matrix of
possible frequencies is returned (and nothing printed).  Here is one
way, I don't say it is the most efficient but it works for moderate
cases:  

enummulti <- function(k, n) {
  # k = number of categories
  # n = total count
  if(n == 0) return(matrix(0, 1, k))
  if(k == 1) return(n)
  E <- NULL
  for(i in 0:n)
    E <- rbind(E, cbind(i, Recall(k-1, n-i)))
  E
}

With large cases you are pretty well snookered whatever way you do it!

Bill Venables.

messages.body_plain:
Apologies for not summarizing. (I mistakenly thought the solutions were 
coming to me via S-news, and therefore available to others.)  As usual, 
there is more than one way to accomplish a goal in S+.  Not all of the 
solutions below work in all versions of S+.

Many thanks to Patrick Connelly, Remy van de Ven, Erin Hodgess, Rod 
Tjoelker,  Nick Ellis, John Bremnes, Bert Gunter, Carlisle Thacker, and 
Shawn Boles for their superfast help!!

Todd

Original message:

I would like to delete from a dataframe certain rows specified by rownames. 
I create an object (e.g., delete.row.names) that is a list of row numbers 
from my dataframe (e.g., temp) that satisfy my criteria for removal. I 
would then like to delete those rows by writing something like

temp[-(temp.row.names), ] but a unary minus is not allowed for data of mode 
character.

I have tried a few variations that do not work either. Any help would be 
appreciated.

I am using S+ 3.3 Win98.

Solutions:
1.
temp[-match(temp.row.names,row.names(temp)),]
although I think you used temp.row.names in your example, but delete.row.names
in the description of the problem.

2.
temp[-match(temp.row.names,dimnames(temp)[[1]])

3.
temp[!is.element(row.names(temp),unwanted.row.names),]

4.
remove.names <- sample( row.names(x), 5 )
k <- match( remove.names, row.names(x) )
x[-k,]

5.
The following is an explicit example:
ta <- data.frame(X=1:10,Y=letters[1:10])
row.names(ta) <- LETTERS[1:10]
ta[-(match(LETTERS[c(8,5,2)],row.names(ta))),]

6.

messages.subject: [S] OffTopic -- Numerical experts: please make me look smart
messages.subject_clean: [S] OffTopic -- Numerical experts: please make me look smart
messages.body_plain:
My apologies in advance. I recently took part in the exchange shown below.
Before replying to Eliot, I'd like to hear what any numerical experts on this
list think.  

For a number of reasons I won't go into here, I have recently become a
Smalltalk fan.  Smalltalk is good at a lot of things, but one thing it's not
very good for is fast number crunching. (At least not directly.  Like S, you
can call out to compiled C code pretty easily.)  

The basic data type understood by the VW virtual machine is a 32-bit object
pointer.  Two bits of the 32 are used as a tag to (partially) identify the
object's type, so up to three data types can be represented in the object
pointer itself with 30 bits of precision.  (The fourth tag indicates that the
other 30 bits are a pointer.)  For example, a SmallInteger in the 30-bit
range: -2^29 to 2^29 - 1 can be directly represented this way.

There is, of course, no way to represent a 32-bit Float or a 64-bit Double in
only 30 bits, so they must use a "boxed" representation, i.e., the tag bits in
the object pointer of a Double identify it as non-immediate, and the other 30
bits are a pointer to a structure in memory that actually holds the value, as
well as an object header identifying the class, etc.

The result is that operations involving Floats and Doubles are both slow and
memory intensive, relative to C, because of all the copying and converting
that takes place.  

With 64-bit object pointers, life becomes more interesting.  Below, Eliot
Miranda is evidently thinking of a scheme with 4 tag bits leaving 60 bits for
representing a floating point value.  How would you reply to him?

Jeff

----------------------------------------------------------------------
From: Eliot Miranda <eliotm at pacbell.net>
Subject: Re: [VW] Reusing Doubles - learn from Java's mistakes
Newsgroups: comp.lang.smalltalk
Date: Thu, 22 Jun 2000 19:40:02 -0700
Organization: SBC Internet Services
Path: 
bog!uunet!ffx.uu.net!newsfeed.mathworks.com!news.maxwell.syr.edu!news-feeder2.wcg.net!WCG!cyclone-sf.pbi.net!206.13.28.144!news.pacbell.net.POSTED!not-for-mail
Message-ID: <3952CE02.10CEB95 at pacbell.net>
X-Mailer: Mozilla 4.72 [en] (Win98; U)
X-Accept-Language: en
MIME-Version: 1.0
References: <394A05F2.26216BFF at Desk.org> <3950EF42.B2983A48 at pacbell.net> 
<rUg45.12647$dF.553087 at news1.rdc1.il.home.com> 
<hkr45.7033$HD6.211475 at iad-read.news.verio.net> <xmr7lbhy68j.fsf at frb.gov>
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=us-ascii
Content-Transfer-Encoding: 7bit
Lines: 35
NNTP-Posting-Host: 63.200.51.254
X-Complaints-To: abuse at pacbell.net
X-Trace: news.pacbell.net 961728006 63.200.51.254 (Thu, 22 Jun 2000 19:40:06 
PDT)
NNTP-Posting-Date: Thu, 22 Jun 2000 19:40:06 PDT
Xref: bog comp.lang.smalltalk:94706

"Jeffrey J. Hallman" wrote:
> 
> "John Baker" <jlbaker at advbool.com> writes:
> > Mark van Gulik <ghoul6 at home.net> wrote in message
> > > <eliotm at pacbell.net>  wrote:
> > > > Right.  The allocation is done within the float and double primitives.
> > > > For a long time the VW engine on Windows had relatively slow code for
> > > > doing float and double calculations.  There's about a 2x speed-up in
> > > > 5i.1, but that's as fast as our current implementation technology can go
> > > > with doubles.  Interesting things might happen with a 64-bit machine,
> > > > providing the user can live with say 3-bits less precision.
> > >
> > > This may seem insignificant (pun intended), but instead of dropping 3 bits
> > > of precision it probably makes more sense to drop 3 bits from the range
> > > (i.e., the upper bits of the exponent).  8x smaller exponent means the
> > > maximum value will be the eight root of the untagged representation.
> > > Since almost all arithmetic will fall within this "safety net", no 
> > > precision
> > > needs to be lost.  In those cases where the exponent would be out of 
> > > range, a
> > > boxed representation can be substituted (similar to Small/Large integers).
> > >
> > > -Mark
> 
> I do statistics and econometrics, and wish to second Mark's comments.  Far
> better to lose 3 bits of range than 3 bits of precision.  High quality
> numerical libraries usually work with numbers that are normalized to something
> near 1.0, so the range of an IEEE double is not nearly as important as its
> precision.

Interesting problem.  So if we have a 64-bit pointer space with, say, 4
bit tags, and I'll let you have up to 4 of the 16 tags to represent
doubles, what range of the double precision range would you represent
and how?
_______________,,,^..^,,,____________________________

messages.subject: [S] Summary - graphsheet background colour
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to Bert Gunter, Mike Prager, Brad Biggerstaff, Sam Buttrey, and
David Smith for their help in solving this problem.

My original message (where I neglected to mention that I'm somewhat
reluctantly using VirtualPC on an iMAC for reasons beyond my control):
**********************************************************
>Hello,
>
>I'm having an interesting problem using Splus Version 4.0.  If I open a
>graphsheet, either just by issuing a "plot" command or with a
>"graphsheet" command,  I initially get a blue graphsheet window which
>has a reddish box in the centre.  As soon as a plot is produced in this
>window, the entire background assumes this disagreeable reddish
>colour.  I can fix this either by clicking on the plot and fixing the fill
>colour in the box which appears, or by using this command:
>
>guiModify("CompositeObject",Name="GSD2$1",FillColor="Transparent")
>
>but how can I get this not to happen in the first place?  I've looked at the
>various places where one might expect to find something that needs setting
up,
>but to no avail.  In particular, when I go down the menu path
>Options, Graphs Styles, Color, Fill Color, none of the 10 fill colours shown
>are the reddish-brown which is appearing in my graphsheet window.
>
>Any advice would be greatly appreciated.
>
>Anona Thorne
**********************************************************

David Smith's response:
**********************************************************
A bug in S-PLUS 4.0 (which has long since been fixed) could cause corruption
to the _Prefs directory (found in your S-PLUS home folder) which resulted in
this behaviour.  A short-term solution is to delete the entire _Prefs
directory and re-start S-PLUS.  This restores all the default settings for
graphs, menus and toolbars (thus removing any other changes you might have
made).  The best solution is to upgrade to S-PLUS 2000 which fixes this bug.

# David Smith

--
David M Smith <dsmith at splus.mathsoft.com>
S-PLUS Product Marketing Manager, MathSoft DAPD, Seattle WA
Tel: +1 (206) 283 8802 x360
Fax: +1 (206) 283 0347
**********************************************************

Summary of Solutions:
**********************************************************
1.  The best solution, as suggested by David Smith of MathSoft, is to
upgrade to S-PLUS 2000, where this problem doesn't exist.  Although that will
happen in our office reasonably soon, we hope, for the moment one of the other
solutions will have to suffice.

2.  As suggested by David Smith, Bert Gunter, and Brad Biggerstaff,
delete (or rename) the entire _Prefs directory and re-start S-PLUS.
This restores all the default settings for graphs, menus and toolbars
(thus removing any other changes you might have made).  Brad suggested
also making a backup copy of your _Prefs directory so that if this
happens again you won't have to reset the defaults.  Great idea; I did this
immediately after fixing things.
 
3.  Mike Prager suggested doing the following.  Fix a graph, then bring up the
context (RMB) menu (which in my case was the Options menu), and click on "Save
Composite Object as Default".  This seems to be a very nice simple fix, though 
of
course, when faced with a corrupt file I wonder what else might be wrong with
it other than the behaviour I see at the moment.

Sam Buttrey suggested a variant on this, which is to get the graph to
be the colors that you want, then choose "Options | Save Window
Size/Properties as Default".  Interestingly, after I tried "Save
Composite Object as Default" as described immediately above, the next
time I looked at the Options menu, the last line had changed from that
description to "Save Window Size/Properties as Default".  My guess is
that what you get in the menu must depend on what you have open and
where the mouse is, etc..
**********************************************************

Mike Prager also enclosed the following helpful suggestion:
**********************************************************
By the way, there is a command equivalent to the menu operation, as there 
is to every menu operation in S-Plus.  If you look at the History window, 
you will see it.  Also, here is a bit of code from a script of mine that 
draws a specific graph:

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Note: var.name is a character value set earlier in the script.
# Open a graphsheet:
guiClose("GraphSheet", var.name)
graphsheet(Name = var.name, print.background = T, color.scheme ="Trellis 
Black on White")

#  Make sure the visible margin of the graphsheet is filled:
guiModifyDefaults("CompositeObject", FillColor = "User14")
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
 
Note that it closes the g.s. first, because if you try to open one that's 
already open, it causes poorly handled S-Plus errors.  Then it opens it and 
sets some options, then sets the fill color.  I am not sure whether it is 
necessary to set this each time (one would think not), but at one time I 
thought I had more predictable results with export.graph() when I set it 
each time.  It can't hurt.
**********************************************************

Again, thanks to all who replied.  

Anona Thorne
Canadian HIV Trials Network
Vancouver, B.C.
Canada

messages.subject: Re: [S] noncentral inverse chisquare
messages.body_plain:
At 04:58 PM 26/06/00 -0400, Joseph F Lucke wrote:
>
>Does anyone know of a noncentral inverse chisquare function for S+?
>This would be a function like qchisq(p,df,ncp).  Currently qchisq does
>not have a noncentrality parameter.

This is a totally non-helpful reply, unfortunately.

I have never heard of one and I think the reason may be because the
percentage points of the non-central chi-squared distribution are rarely of
much interest.

What is of much more interest, though, is a different kind of inverse
function.  For power (or sample size) calculations you need to know the
value of the non-centrality parameter that makes  1-pchisq(X, dfr, ncp) =
beta, where X is the central chi-squared 0.95 (or whatever) cutoff point,
fixed.  I'd be interested to know if anyone had automated this calculation,
though for a single value (generally all you need) you can usually do it
pretty quickly using uniroot() or even just trial-and-error.

messages.subject: [S] specifying font numbers in SPlus 2000 (summary)
messages.body_plain:
THanks to LH Lam and David Smith for answering my question on specifying
font numbers in Splus 2000. The original question is appended below.

To do this from the command line, one can use the commands 
graphsheet or GuiModify. Here is an example -- you must be
careful to spell the font names correctly!! 

graphsheet(width = 8, height = 10, fonts = c("times new roman", 
                "times new roman bold", "times new roman italic", 
                "times new roman bold italic", "arial", "arial bold", 
                "arial italic", "arial bold italic"))

If the graphics window is already open, and one wants to modify it, you can
do so using the GuiModify commands. For example:

guiModify( "GraphSheet", Name = "GS1", CommandFont1 = "Garamond") 

I found the help file for guiModify to be cryptic, at best. 

People work in different ways, but for me, working on the command line is
preferable to using the gui-interface. 26 letters do a lot for me and I
have a hard time remembering what all those icons mean. 

Both LH Lam and David Smith mentioned that the way to discover the
GuiModify command is to use the gui (right click on the graph and go to
options), make the changes you want, and then examine what SPlus did in the
command history window.  In my opinion, this is a bit arcane and is not a
suitable substitute for well-written and well- indexed help files.

messages.subject: [S] Report Window anomalies
messages.body_plain:
S-Plus 2000 on Windows NT 4.0

Here are one probable bug, an incompatibility, and some wishes relating to 
S-Plus 2000 Report files.  Comments or suggestions from motivated list 
readers are welcome.

Bug: Font changes in an S-Plus Report only "stick" beyond the point that a 
font attribute is changed.  For example, in a report window, I changed the 
font for all text to "Monospaced 821", then set a few lines in the middle 
of the file to bold, as well.  After I saved and re-opened the file in 
S-Plus, the font in text before the bold lines had reverted to Courier 
New.  Something like this has been a persistent problem since the release 
of S-Plus 2000, and not just with that particular font.

Incompatibility: In last November's discussion of the SRP format used for 
S-Plus 2000 reports (i.e., documents created with the Report window), David 
Smith of Mathsoft stated:

>> 1. Any '.srp' file can be opened directly by WordPerfect (but not by 
Word). <<

To the contrary, I have found that WordPerfect 8, at least, has no idea 
what to do with any .SRP file I've asked it to open.  Am I missing 
something here, did David misspeak, or is the very latest version of 
WordPerfect needed for this?

Indeed, not one Windows file viewer or file manager I've tried can handle 
an SRP file.  Mathsoft called it an "off-the-shelf" format, but it seems 
that everyone else has left it ON the shelf.  The only apparent way to edit 
or view an S-Plus Report is to open it in S-Plus.  I still find that at 
odds with the concept of a report, which to me is a means of exchanging 
information.

Wishes:  I still would like the option to save a report with graphics in 
the widely compatible RTF format; I understand that option used to be 
standard.  I'd like at least simple formatting controls, like Ctrl-B for 
bold and Ctrl-I for italics.  I'd like to be able to resize a graphic in a 
report window without changing aspect ratio by using Ctrl-drag or 
Shift-drag on the mouse.  I'd like to be able to import (NOT using OLE, 
DDE, or other configuration- or platform-specific methods) a report file 
into a major (or minor) word processor.

I wish for these things because, given all versions of Windows's MDI GUI, 
in which an application's "master window" blocks convenient access to other 
applications, the Report Window is the best tool I've found so far to 
compile a record of work done in S-Plus.  It is especially nice to be able 
to combine text and graphics in a continuous stream.  The concept is great 
-- I just ask for more refinement.  I was hoping that after last November's 
discussion we might have some of it soon.

--
Michael Prager      <Mike.Prager at noaa.gov>
NOAA Beaufort Laboratory
Beaufort, North Carolina  28516  USA

messages.subject: [S] greek letters in axis labels with mtext
messages.subject_clean: [S] greek letters in axis labels with mtext
messages.body_plain:
S+2000 R2, Win98

I searched the archive and did not find the following approach,
so I thought I would post it.

I _really_ needed greek letters in axis labels.  No time to 
install/learn pstricks, and the GUI wouldn't let me mix subscripts
and greek and text, at least as near as I could tell from reading
what documentation I could find.

So I kludged something from mtext that gives me a "beta hat"
with a subscript "T" and a couple gammas with subscripts.

Bruce McCullough

- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - 
# use "oma" to ensure enough room to plot axis labels
par(oma=c(1,1,1,1))
# put up a null plot
plot(0,0,xlim=c(-2730,3777),ylim=c(-120,95), ylab="",xlab="",type="n")
mtext("COST -                NB",side=2,line=3,font=1,outer=F,at=-30,srt=90)
# font=8 gives me greek letters, so b is beta and g is gamma
mtext("(b  / g    )",side=2,line=3,font=8,outer=F,at=-20,srt=90)
mtext(" ^",side=2,line=3.5,outer=F,at=-32,srt=90)
mtext("_",side=2,line=3.8,outer=F,at=-16,srt=90)
mtext("T",side=2,line=2.5,font=1,outer=F,at=-27,srt=90,cex=0.8)
mtext("NB",side=2,line=2.5,font=1,outer=F,at=-12,srt=90,cex=0.8)

mtext("NB -                  BO",side=1,line=3,font=1,outer=F,at=1000,srt=0)
mtext("(g    / g     )",side=1,line=3,font=8,outer=F,at=1100,srt=0)
mtext("_",side=1,line=2.2,font=1,outer=F,at=1145,srt=0)
mtext("_",side=1,line=2.2,font=1,outer=F,at=816,srt=0)
mtext("NB",side=1,line=4,font=1,outer=F,at=965,srt=0,cex=0.8)
mtext("BO",side=1,line=4,font=1,outer=F,at=1300,srt=0,cex=0.8)
