> appropriate parameters.

does this help?  not sure about ML for weibull.

fitter.gamma <- function(x, ml.shape = T)
{
        #
        # fits a two-parameter gamma distribution to x, and plots a
comparison
        # of the empirical and estimated distribution functions.  This
uses
        # the (mean, shape) parameterization rather than the usual
(scale, 
        # shape) one, i.e., mu==alpha*beta, nu==beta.
        #
        # the ml.shape arg allows the shape parameter to be fit as per
        # McCullagh and Nelder's moment estimation suggestion for data
        # with zeroes.
        #
        x <- sort(x[!is.na(x)])
        n <- length(x)
        #
        #
        # compute MLEs for mean and shape
        mu <- mean(x)
        assign("sbar", mean(x), frame = 1)
        assign("logsbar", mean(log(x)), frame = 1)
        fun <- function(nu)
        {
 - nu * logsbar - nu * log(nu/sbar) + nu + lgamma(nu)
        }
        if(ml.shape == T)
                nu <- nlmin(fun, 1)$x
        else nu <- (mu * mu)/var(x)
        print(c(mu, nu))
        #
        #
        # compute and plot the empirical distribution function
        S <- sort.list(x)/n
        for(i in unique(x[duplicated(x)])) {
                which <- x == i
                S[which] <- max(S[which])
        }
        xmin <- x[1] - 0.05 * (x[n] - x[1])
        xmax <- x[n] + 0.05 * (x[n] - x[1])
        plot(c(xmin, rep(x, rep(2, n)), xmax), rep(c(0, S), rep(2, n +
1)),
                type = "l", main = 
                "Empirical vs. Parametric Gamma Distribution", xlab = 
                "quantile", ylab = "Cumulative Probability")
        #
        #
        # compute and plot the parametric estimate of the distribution
function
        xx <- seq(xmin, xmax, length = 100)
        lines(xx, pgamma2(xx, shape = nu, mean = mu))
        invisible()
}

"fit.gamma"<-
function(data, test = T, minimizer = "ms", plot = T)
{
# written by Franz Mueter, last modified: 1/28/97
# function to fit gamma distribution with shape parameter alpha
# and scale parameter lambda to a data set. Method of moment and
# maximum likelihood estimates are returned.
# data          vector of values: X1, X2, .....Xn
# test          if TRUE, a Kolmogorof-Smirnof Goodness of fit test is done
#               and results are printed 
# minimizer     should be one of "ms" or "nlminb", try nlminb (which adds a
lower bound)
#               if ms doesn't work
# plot          if TRUE, a histogram is plotted with the MLE fit
#
# method of moment estimates:
        xbar <- mean(data)
        sigma2 <- var(data)
        aa <- xbar^2/sigma2
        ll <- xbar/sigma2       #
# maximize likelihood using ms():
        if(minimizer == "ms") {
                assign("N", length(data), frame = 0)
                assign("S1", sum(log(data)), frame = 0)
                assign("S2", sum(data), frame = 0)
                MLE <- ms( ~  - N * alpha * log(lambda) - (alpha - 1) * S1 + 
                        lambda * S2 + N * lgamma(alpha), start = list(alpha = 
                        aa, lambda = ll))
                loglik <-  - MLE$value
        }
        else {
                if(minimizer == "nlminb") {
                        MLE <- nlminb(c(aa, ll), loglik.gamma, lower = c(0, 0), 
                                x = data)
                        loglik <-  - MLE[[2]]
                }
                else stop("minimizers currently supported are 'ms' and 'nlminb'"
                                )
        }
        names(loglik) <- "log likelihood"
        estimates <- list(data = deparse(substitute(data)), MOM.estimates = 
                cbind(alpha = aa, lambda = ll), MLE.estimates = c(MLE$
                parameters, loglik), minimizer = minimizer)     #
# plot fit:
        if(plot) {
                hist(data, nclass = sqrt(length(data)), prob = T)
                xa <- seq(0.01, max(data), max(data)/100)
                lines(xa, dgamma(xa * MLE$parameters[2], MLE$parameters[1]) * 
                        MLE$parameters[2], lwd = 2)
                title(paste("Histogram of ", deparse(substitute(data)), 
                        " with gamma fit\n(maximum likelihood estimate)"))
        }
# Goodness of fit tests (Kolmogorof-Smirnof)
        if(test) {
                cat("Goodness of fit test for MOM estimates:")
                print(ks.gof(data * ll, distr = "gamma", shape = aa))
                cat("Goodness of fit test for MLE estimates:")
                print(ks.gof(data * MLE$parameters[2], distr = "gamma", shape
                         = MLE$parameters[1]))
        }
        estimates
}
"fit.weibull"<-
function(data, test = T, minimizer = "ms", delta = 1, lambda = 1)
{
# written by Franz Mueter, last modified: 2/16/97
# function to fit weibull distribution with shape parameter alpha
# and scale parameter lambda to a data set by maximum likelihood
# data          vector of values: X1, X2, .....Xn
# test          if TRUE, a Kolmogorof-Smirnof Goodness of fit test is done
#               and results are printed 
# minimizer     should be one of "ms" or "nlminb", try nlminb (which adds a
lower bound)
#               if ms doesn't work
# delta, lambda         initial parameter values
#
# maximize likelihood using ms():
        if(minimizer == "ms") {
                assign("N", length(data), frame = 0)
                assign("S", sum(log(data)), frame = 0)
                MLE <- ms( ~ N * delta * log(lambda) - N * log(delta) - (delta 
- 
                        1) * S + lambda^( - delta) * sum(data^delta), start = 
                        list(delta = delta, lambda = lambda))
                loglik <-  - MLE$value
        }
        else {
                if(minimizer == "nlminb") {
                        MLE <- nlminb(c(delta, lambda), loglik.weibull, lower
                                 = c(0, 0), x = data)
                        loglik <-  - MLE[[2]]
                }
                else stop("minimizers currently supported are 'ms' and 'nlminb'"
                                )
        }
        names(loglik) <- "log-likelihood"
        estimates <- list(data = deparse(substitute(data)), MLE.estimates = c(
                MLE$parameters, loglik), minimizer = minimizer) #
# plot fit
        hist(data, nclass = sqrt(N), prob = T)
        x <- seq(0, max(data), max(data)/100)
        lines(x, dweibull(x, MLE$parameters[1], MLE$parameters[2]), lwd = 2)
        title(paste("Weibull fit to ", deparse(substitute(data)), " data"))     
        # Goodness of fit tests (Kolmogorof-Smirnof)
        if(test) {
                cat("Goodness of fit test for MLE estimates:")
                print(ks.gof(data, distr = "weibull", shape = MLE$parameters[1],
                        scale = MLE$parameters[2]))
        }
        estimates
}

messages.subject: [S] AI & Statistics 2001: Deadline 10 July
messages.body_plain:
Eighth International Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and
 Statistics

 January 3-6, 2001, Hyatt Hotel, Key West, Florida

 http://www.ai.mit.edu/conferences/aistats2001/

 SUBMISSION DEADLINE: midnight July 10, 2000 (PST)

 This is the eighth in a series of workshops which have brought
 together researchers in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and in Statistics
 to discuss problems of mutual interest.

 To encourage interaction and a broad exchange of ideas, the
 presentations will be limited to about 20 discussion papers in single
 session meetings over three days (Jan. 4-6). Focused poster sessions
 will provide the means for presenting and discussing the remaining
 research papers. Papers for poster sessions will be treated equally
 with papers for presentation in publications.  Attendance at the
 workshop will not be limited.

 The three days of research presentations will be preceded by a day of
 tutorials (Jan. 3). These are intended to expose researchers in each
 field to the methodology and techniques used in other related areas.

 The Eighth workshop especially encourages submissions related to the
 following workshop themes in the interface between information
 retrieval and statistics:

  Statistical natural language processing
  Game theory
  Missing information; unlabeled examples
  Error correcting codes

 In addition, papers on all aspects of the interface between AI &
 Statistics are strongly encouraged.

 Submission Requirements:

 Electronic submission of abstracts is required. The abstracts (up to 4
 pages in length) should be submitted through the AI and Statistics
 Conference Management page supported by Microsoft Research. More
 specific instructions are available at

 http://cmt.research.microsoft.com/AISTATS2001/

 Submissions will be considered if they are received by midnight July
 10, 2000 (PST).  Please indicate the theme and/or the topic(s) your abstract
 addresses. Receipt of all submissions will be confirmed via electronic
 mail. Acceptance notices will be emailed by September 1, 2000.

 Preliminary papers (up to 12 pages, double column) must be received by
 November 1, 2000. These preliminary papers will be copied and
 distributed at the workshop.

 Program Chairs:

 Thomas Richardson, University of Washington, tsr at stat.washington.edu
 Tommi Jaakkola, MIT, tommi at ai.mit.edu

messages.body_plain:
I believe you can use censorReg to fit these distributions (fit a model with
only intercept), even though you may not have censored data.  You might also
want to look at Meeker's SLIDA module for Splus on Windows.

Chi^2 goodness-of-fit just test whether a particular distribution is a good
fit for the data.  It does not give parameter estimates.  If I'm not
mistaken, the way it works is by dividing the data into several intervals
and compare observed counts in each interval against what would be expected
if the data came from the target distribution, not unlike the chi^2 test for
contingency tables.

messages.subject: RE: [S] Report Window anomalies
messages.body_plain:
I would like to point out that I know of at least two packages that do a
pretty decent job of collecting text/graphics output: JMP 4.0 (just
released) and SYSSTAT (9.0?).  Both will let user save something like the
report window as HTML, which I think might be even more useful/universal
than RTF.  In JMP4, the user has option to choose the format of the graphics
to use in the HTML (jpeg/png, I think).

I'm actually not familiar with either of the two packages, but I think this
should be something that MathSoft can consider.

messages.subject: [S] SUMMARY: (likelihoods &) weights in glm
messages.body_plain:
Tim Hesterberg wrote   

>The following draft documentation relates to lm; it may help
>you with glm and gam.  I'd also appreciate if you tell me about any
>problems you find with this, or what you learn about glm and gam.
>My goal is to have good documentation on the effect of weights in
>various modeling functions.

This relates to a more general concern (raised a year or so ago) about
likelihoods being under-emphasized in SPlus. 

If you want to know/see what the "weights option does" in a glm or gam you
need to look how the weights modify the likelihood quantities on which the
glm/gam estimates/tests are based. This amongst others reason is why
likelihood output should be readily available to the user. (Likelihood
quantities are much, much simpler in lm and perhaps can be neglected)

That there is a real risk of mis-interpreting the use of the "weight option"
see
Lancet 1998 Aug 22;352(9128):609-13 Does quality of reports of randomised
trials affect estimates of intervention efficacy reported in meta-analyses?
Moher D, Pham B, Jones A, Cook DJ, Jadad AR, Moher M, Tugwell P, Klassen TP

Also we need to know what purpose the weights are meant to accomplish - as
there are more possible uses than dealing with precision. 
(A neat variant of dealing with both precision and bias can be seen in 
DR Cox. Combination of data. In: Encyclopedia of Statistical Science 2,
edited by S Kotz and NL Johnson, New York:Wiley, 1982.)

Hope this may of some interest
p.s. (as usual) the essential "hints" were in Brian Ripley's post on this
thread

Keith O'Rourke
Statistician, Department of Surgery and Clinical Epidemiology Unit
University of Ottawa/ Ottawa Hospital

messages.subject: [S] Summary - Monte Carlo in S+
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

here is my original question
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 I need to set up a Monte Carlo experiment
to evaluate a regression. How do I set up the correlations between the vectors
drawn from the distributions? I also need to truncate the simulated values at
certain levels, for example, one of the vectors needs to be drawn from the log
normal distribution and needs to be truncated at the upper limit of 100. I would
be very grateful for any pointers or canned code. I shall summarize.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
And here are the answers. The "rmvnorm" function appears very useful, although
it did not quite provide me with what I needed. We might try to look into the
Environmental Stats module.
Thanks to Kevin Brand and Rick Detmars.

Sarada

_________________________________________________________________________________________________
Majumder,

You should check out rmvnorm as a way to generate multivariate normal data
according to your desired covariance structure.  Note, exponentiating your
random draws from rmvnorm will yield lognormal data, however, achieving a
desired covariance structure in antilog space is difficult.

Truncation is simple,

# for example,
x_rlnorm(1000, meanlog = 0, sdlog = 1)
# this yields 1000 LN distributed samples with GM=1 and GSD=exp(1)
# to truncate
x_x[x<100] # this will keep only those x's less than 100.

hope this helps,

cheers,
Kevin
___________________________________________________________________________________________________
All of those capabilities are available in the Environmental Stats for
S-Plus Module.  This module was developed by Steve Millard at PSI, which
was recently acquired by Mathsoft.

See www.probstatinfo.com for info on the EnvStats module.  According to the
web site,  Region 10 of the EPA is using this module.

messages.subject: Re: [S] Error in nlme (Sp2000)
messages.body_plain:
Dear In-Sun,

> I have very recently acquired S-plus 2000 (revised version
> 2) and also obtained a book called "Mixed-Effects Models in
> S and S-plus" by Pinheiro and Bates.
> 
> In the book, one of their examples using Wafer data which is
> presented as far below, proves that "fm3Wafer" which uses
> more general variance covariance matrix structure for the
> random effects are better than "fm2Wafer" which uses
> diagonal matrices.
> 
> However, my program decides to give me an error message (as
> far below) for the last bit (fm3Wafer) instead of the proper
> results which is presented in the book.
> 
> I acknowledge that nlme versions might different from the
> one in Splus2000 and the one used in the book, but shouldn't
> it work in the most recent version anyway?
> 
> I will very much appreciate if someone would provide me a
> solution to resolve this nonsense.
. . .
> Warning messages:
>   Warning in log((val + 1)/(1 - val)): NAs generated
> Error in .C("natural_pd",: subroutine natural_pd: 1 missing
> value(s) in argument 3

The error message indicates that the problem is in the calculation of
the approximate variance-covariance matrix of the estimates, which
uses numerical derivatives and a "natural" unconstrained
parameterization. This happens because the fm3Wafer model has a
"nearly overparameterized" variance-covariance matrix for the random
effects, which, in this case, causes the estimates to be too close to
the boundary of the parameter space (the rather obscure warning
message you get indicates that the calculation of the logit
transformation of the correlation coefficient produces an NA, which
occurs if the increment added to produce the numerical derivatives
took the value outside the (-1,1) interval).

Anyway, the numerical derivative calculations are dependent on the
platform on which you are running S-PLUS. The example in the book was
produced on S-PLUS 3.4 running on an Iris 5.1 SGI machine. The version
in S-PLUS 2000 is able to get convergence, but not to produce the
numerical Hessian. The solution is simple: turn off the calculation of
the numerical derivatives by including

        control = list(apVar = F)

in the call to update (used to produce fm3Wafer).

Hope this solves the problem. Let me know if you still have problems
fitting the model.

Best,
--Jose'

messages.subject: [S] bootstraps with spatially aotocorrelated data
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This is not strictly a S+ question. I suppose it could be implemented in any
software.

I have some data on which we performed some preliminary regression. The errors
are spatially autocorrelated (checked via Moran's I statistic). Tried out a
separate model (SAR etc.) but the explanatory power of the more complicated
models are none better than the OLS. The concern is with the coefficients and
the significance of the coefficients. Is it feasible to perform bootstrapping
with the spatially autocorrelated dataset to look at the distribution of
parameters? I know bootstrapping is usually not done on time series, do the same
restrictions apply? Has anybody done anything similar?

Sincerely

Sarada

messages.subject_clean: [S] Two new public courses from CSIRO
messages.body_plain:
> CSIRO Mathematical & Information Sciences will be offering two interesting
> new courses before the end of 2000:
> 
> Design, Monitoring and Analysis of Group Sequential Clinical Trials 
> with Dr John Kittelson from the University of Otago NZ, 3 - 4 August
> 
> and
> 
> Advanced Programming in S-PLUS
> with Dr Bill Venables, CSIRO Mathematical & Information Sciences, 14 - 15
> November
> 
> Both courses will be held at CSIRO on the Macquarie University campus in
> Sydney.
> More information and booking forms are available from our web site at
> http://www.cmis.csiro.au/S-PLUS, but summaries follow.
> 
> Design, Monitoring and Analysis of Group Sequential Clinical Trials
> 
> Course Description:
> Increasingly, clinical trials are conducted using group sequential methods
> in order to address the ethical and efficiency issues that arise when
> performing experiments with human volunteers.  The design, conduct, and
> analysis of a sequential clinical trial is necessarily more involved than
> that for a clinical trial in which the data would only be analysed at the
> end of the study.  In this short course we present the additional issues
> that must be considered when conducting a group sequential trial.  
> The group sequential methods are illustrated using S+SeqTrial, a module
> for the design, monitoring, and analysis of clinical trials.  Course
> participants will receive hands-on instruction in the use of  S+SeqTrial
> to perform the various statistical tasks necessary from start to finish in
> the conduct of a clinical trial.
> Presenter:
> Dr John Kittelson is a lecturer in biostatistics at the University of
> Otago, Dunedin, New Zealand. His research interests include frameworks for
> unification of group sequential trial designs, and methods for evaluating
> design properties as they relate to clinical questions.  John has worked
> as a biostatistician since 1986, and with group sequential clinical trials
> since 1990.  The design routines of S+SeqTrial are based on the unified
> family of designs described by Kittelson and Emerson (Biometrics, 1999).
> Costs:
> Commercial:   $1000
> Non profit:     $900
> Academic:       $900
> 
> The fee includes lunch, refreshments and course materials.  The price does

plot(x,y)

will give you a plot as well.

messages.subject: [S] Summary - Shaprro-Wilk test
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to Marc R. Feldesman, John Paul and
Andy White for their help!

Here is my question
-------------
Could someone tell me whether there is a
function for Shaprro-Wilk test for normality in
S-plus?
-------------

Below are the answers:
(I attached the file Marc sent to me.)
---
1)
Attached is an S-Plus script file for doing the Shapiro-Wilk test.  I got 
it from the CMU S library server about a year ago.

Hope this helps.
    [ Part 2, Application/OCTET-STREAM (Name: "shapiro.wilk.test.ssc")  ]
    [ 2.5KB. ]
    [ Not Shown. Use the "V" command to view or save this part. ]

    [ Part 3: "Attached Text" ]

Dr. Marc R. Feldesman
email:  feldesmanm at pdx.edu
email:  feldesman at ibm.net
fax:    503-725-3905
----
---
2)
The following is a function I pulled off the StatLib Library.  I
"discovered"
this function thorough an earlier inquiry to S-News.

John Paul
Atlantic Ecology Division
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
Narragansett, Rhode Island
U.S.A.
paul.john at epa.gov

> shapiro.wilk.test
function(x)
{
#             "shapiro.wilk.test"
#
# This function is an S version of the procedure described by
# J. P. Royston (1982) in "An Extension of Shapiro and Wilk's
# W Test for Normality to Large Samples", Applied Statistics,
# Vol. 31, No. 2, pp 115-124.
#
     n <- length(x)
     index <- 1:n
     m <- qnorm((index - 0.375)/(n + 0.25))
     y <- sort(x)
     mu <- mean(y)
     SSq <- sum((y - mu)^2)
     astar <- 2 * m
     ends <- c(1, n)
     astar.p <- astar[ - ends]
     if(n <= 20)
     m <- n - 1
     else m <- n
     if(m < 20)
     aa <- gamma(0.5 * (m + 1))/(sqrt(2) *
     gamma(0.5 * m + 1))
     else {
     f1 <- (6 * m + 7)/(6 * m + 13)
     f2 <- exp(1)/(m + 2)
     f3 <- (m + 1)/(m + 2)
     f3 <- f3^(m - 2)
     aa <- f1 * sqrt(f2 * f3)
     }
     astar.1 <- (aa * sum(astar.p^2))/(1 - 2 * aa)
     astar.1 <- sqrt(astar.1)
     astar[1] <-  - astar.1
     astar[n] <- astar.1
     A <- astar/sqrt(sum(astar^2))
     W <- (sum(A * y)^2)/SSq
    if(n <= 20) {
     u <- log(n) - 3
     lambda <- 0.118898 + 0.133414 * u +
     0.327907 * u^2
     logmu <- -0.37542 - 0.492145 * u -
     1.124332 * u^2 - 0.199422 * u^3
     logsigma <- -3.155805 + 0.729399 * u +
     3.01855 * u^2 + 1.5558776 * u^3
     }
     if(n > 20) {
     u <- log(n) - 5
     lambda <- 0.480385 + 0.318828 * u +
     0.0241665 * u^3 + 0.00879701 *
     u^4 + 0.002989646 * u^5
     logmu <- -1.91487 - 1.37888 * u -
     0.04189209 * u^2 + 0.1066339 *
     u^3 - 0.03513666 * u^4 -
     0.01504614 * u^5
     logsigma <- -3.83538 - 1.015807 * u - 0.331885 *
     u^2 + 0.1773538 * u^3 - 0.01638782 * u^4 -
     0.03215018 * u^5 + 0.003852646 * u^6
     }
     mu <- exp(logmu)
     sigma <- exp(logsigma)
     y <- (1 - W)^lambda
     z <- (y - mu)/sigma
     p <- 1 - pnorm(z)
     if(n < 7) {
     warning("n is to small for this program
to correctly estimate p"
     )
     p <- NA
     }
     if(n > 2000) {
     warning("n is too large for this program
 to correctly estimate p"
   )
     p <- NA
     }
     out <- list(W = W, n = n, p = p)
     out
}
-------

3)
You should get quite  a few answers and I would appreciate your summary of
them. Here's my own log of past responses (see attached refs to older
emails).

Aloha from Hawaii, 
Andy White

Date: Tue, 17 Aug 1999 18:16:14 -1000
From: Peter B. Mandeville <mandevip at uaslp.mx>
To: S-news <s-news at wubios.wustl.edu>
Subject: Re: [S] Shapiro-Wilks' test

I coded the Shapiro-Francia test which handles from 5 to 5000 observations
from 

        Patrick Royston
        1993 A Pocket-Calculator Algorithm for the Shapiro-Francia Test
for
                Non-Normality: An Application to Medicine. Statistics in
Medicine vol
12, 181-184
        1991 Estimating Departure from Normality. Statistics in Medicine.
                vol 10, 1283-1293

 1983 A Simple Method for Evaluating the Shapiro-Francia W' Test of 
                Non-Normality. The Statistician 32 (1983) 297-300

and the D'Agostino tests from

        Ralph B. D'Agostino, Albert Belanger, and Ralph B. D'Agostino, Jr.
        1990 A Suggestion for Using Powerful and Informative Tests of
Normality.
                The American Statistician, November 1990, Vol. 44, No. 4

for testing normality in R. They should work in S plus with the exception
of hist which I believe is specific to R but which I believe is available
in MASS from Venables y Ripley 1997.

# NORMALIDAD

# Peter
NORMAL <- function(data){

  cat("NORMALIDAD\n")
    DAGOSTINO(data)
    SHAPIRO.FRANCIA(data)
    EDA.SHAPE(data)
}

# Mathsoft 1998:45
EDA.SHAPE <- function(data){
    dest <- density(data)
    hist(data,xlim=range(dest$x),xlab="x",ylab="density",freq=F)
    lines(dest,lty=2,col="red")
    boxplot(data,main="Diagrama de Caja")
    qqnorm(data)
    qqline(data)
    SYMPLOT(data)
}

# Lee 1996:33-34
MOMENTS <- function(data,r) sum((data-mean(data))^r)/length(data)

# Peter
SKEW <- function(data)
MOMENTS(data,3)/(MOMENTS(data,2)*sqrt(MOMENTS(data,2)))

# Peter
KURTOSIS <-
function(data) MOMENTS(data,4)/(MOMENTS(data,2)*MOMENTS(data,2))

# Peter
OUTLIERS <- function(data){
    cat("OUTLIERS\n")
    x <- FIVE(data)
    n <- length(data)
    cat("  CI PARA OUTLIERS:",x[1],"\n")
    for(j in 1:n)
        if(data[j]<x[1]) cat("    Obs",j,":",data[j],"\n")
    cat("  CS PARA OUTLIERS:",x[5],"\n")
    for(j in 1:n)
if(data[j]<x[1]) cat("    Obs",j,":",data[j],"\n")
    cat("  CS PARA OUTLIERS:",x[5],"\n")
    for(j in 1:n)
        if(data[j]>x[5]) cat("    Obs",j,":",data[j],"\n")
}

# D'Agostino, Belanger and D'Agostino 1990:316-321
DAGOSTINO <- function(data){
    cat("  PRUEBAS DE D'AGOSTINO\n")
    n <- length(data)
    cat("    SIMETRIA\n")
    cat("      COEFICIENTE DE SIMETRIA:",sqrtb1 <- SKEW(data),"\n")
    if(n>8){
        y <- sqrtb1*sqrt((n+1)*(n+3)/(6*(n-2)))
        beta2 <- 3*(n*n+27*n-70)*(n+1)*(n+3)/((n-2)*(n+5)*(n+7)*(n+9))
        w <- sqrt(-1+sqrt(2*(beta2-1)))
        delta <- 1/sqrt(log(w))
 ALPHA <- sqrt(2/(w*w-1))
        cat("      ZETA CALCULADA:",zb1 <-
delta*log(y/ALPHA+sqrt((y/ALPHA)^2+1)),"\n")
        cat("      PROBABILIDAD:",2*(1-pnorm(abs(zb1))),"\n")
    }else
        cat("    LA PRUEBA DE SESGO REQUIERE POR LO MENOS 9
REPETICIONES\n")
    cat("    KURTOSIS\n")
    cat("      COEFICIENTE DE KURTOSIS:",b2 <- KURTOSIS(data),"\n")
    if(n>19){
       meanb2 <- 3*(n-1)/(n+1)
       varb2 <- 24*n*(n-2)*(n-3)/((n+1)*(n+1)*(n+3)*(n+5))
       x <- (b2-meanb2)/sqrt(varb2)
       moment <-
6*(n*n-5*n+2)/((n+7)*(n+9))*sqrt(6*(n+3)*(n+5)/(n*(n-2)*(n-3)))
       a <- 5+8/moment*(2/moment+sqrt(1+4/(moment*moment)))
       cat("      ZETA CALCULADA:",zb2 <-

(1-2/(9*a)-((1-2/a)/(1+x*sqrt(2/(a-4))))^(1/3))/sqrt(2/(9*a)),"\n")
       cat("      PROBABILIDAD:",2*(1-pnorm(abs(zb2))),"\n")
       cat("    OMNIBUS\n")
       cat("      JI-CUADRADA CALCULADA:",k2 <- zb1*zb1+zb2*zb2,"\n")
       cat("      GRADOS DE LIBERTAD: 2\n")
       cat("      PROBABILIDAD:",probji2 <- 1-pchisq(k2,2),"\n")
    }else
       cat("    LAS PRUEBAS DE KURTOSIS Y OMNIBUS REQUIEREN POR LO MENOS
20
REPETICIONES\n")
}

# Royston 1993:183-184
SHAPIRO.FRANCIA <- function(data){
    cat("  PRUEBA DE NORMALIDAD DE SHAPIRO-FRANCIA\n")
    n <- length(data)
    if(n<5 || n>5000)
        cat("    REQUIERE ENTRE 5 Y 5000 REPETICIONES\n")
    else{
 xbar <- mean(data)
        sdata <- sort(data)
        resid <- sdata-xbar
        uniform <- seq(1,n)
        np <- qnorm((uniform-0.375)/(n+0.25))
        cat("    W':",w <-
(sum(np*sdata))^2/(sum(np*np)*sum(resid*resid)),"\n")
        u <- log(n)
        v <- log(u)
        muy <- -1.2725+1.0521*(v-u)
        sigmay <- 1.0308-0.26758*(v+2/u)
        cat("    ZETA CALCULADA:",zeta <- (log(1-w)-muy)/sigmay,"\n")
        cat("    PROBABILIDAD:",probz <- 1-pnorm(zeta),"\n")
    }
}

Peter B.

messages.body_plain:
KDD-2000:
       The Sixth ACM SIGKDD International Conference
          on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining

           August 20-23, 2000, Boston, MA, USA
           Conference Headquarters: World Trade
                 Center and Seaport Hotel

            http://www.acm.org/sigkdd/kdd2000

The KDD conference series is the premiere event for the data
mining community, bringing together more than 800 data mining
professionals from industry and academia (our participation
rates are 60% industry and 40% academia).  For more information
about the conference, please visit
http://www.acm.org/sigkdd/kdd2000.

+--------------------------------+
| KDD-2000 Conference Highlights |
+--------------------------------+

The conference features Research Track keynotes, paper and
poster presentations; Industrial Track keynotes, invited
industrial speakers and presentations; Tutorials; Workshops;
Panels on controversial issues and areas of interest and,
extensive vendor and publisher Exhibits. The conference also
features KDD-Cup, the Fourth International Data Mining Tools
Competition.

Research Track includes Keynote Addresses by:

o Christos H. Papadimitriou, UC-Berkeley, "On Certain Rigorous
  Approaches to Data Mining"
o Jason Catlett, Junkbusters Corp., "Among Those Dark Electronic
  Mills: Privacy and Data Mining"
o Bruce Buchanan, University of Pittsburgh, "Informed Knowledge
  Discovery: Using Prior Knowledge in Discovery Problems"

Industrial Track includes Keynote Addresses by:

o James Goodnight, CEO, SAS, "Decision Support in the Booming
  E-World"
o Michael Saylor, CEO, MicroStrategy, "One to One Relationships
  via Web, Wireless and Voice"

Industrial Track also includes Invited Talks by:

o Matt Cutler, CeIO, NetGenesis, "E-Metrics: Tomorrow's Business
  Metrics Today"
o David Stodder, Editorial Director, Intelligent Enterprise,
  "After the Gold Rush: Data Mining and the New Economy"

KDD-2000 Tutorials:

  The KDD-2000 Tutorial program provides intensive and
  inexpensive training opportunity to participants from industry
  and government.  The timeliness of the proposed topics make them
  of value to academic researchers as well.  Tutorial attendance
  is included with KDD-2000 registration.  Tutorials will occur on
  Sunday, August 20, 2000. The following Tutorials are offered
  this year:

  o Data Mining for HyperText
  o Multidimensional Visualization
  o Knowledge Discovery in Biological Domains
  o Data Mining for Successful Customer Management (CRM)
  o Time Series Similarity Measures
  o High Performance Data Mining

KDD-2000 Workshops:

  The workshops aim at discussing recent research advances in
  focused areas of knowledge discovery and data mining.  They are
  intended to be small and intimate to foster open discussion. The
  following Workshops are offered this year:

  o Web Mining for E-Commerce
  o Distributed and Parallel Knowledge Discovery
  o Multimedia Data Mining
  o Post-Processing in Machine Learning and Data Mining
  o Text Mining

KDD-2000 Panels:

  Panels address new, exciting, and controversial issues in the
  data mining community. The following Panels are offered this
  year:

  o KDD Process Standards
  o Personalization and Data Mining:  Exploring the Synergies
  o Privacy

KDD-Cup-2000:

  The popular KDD Cup competition for applications of data
  mining focuses this year on analysis of web clickstream data
  from an apparel retailer. The awards ceremony for this year's
  winners will be held on Sunday, 8/20 following the conference
  inauguration.

KDD-2000 Exhibits:

  The exhibits will stay open on Monday, 8/21 and Tuesday,
  8/22. A select list of Exhibitors includes:

  Accrue, AIM Learning, Amazon.com, Angoss, Blue Martini, Carat,
  High Tower, i2inc, IBM, K.wiz, Kxen, Marcom, MathSoft,
  Megaputer, Mineit, Multilogic, Salford Systems, Spotfire, SAS,
  SPSS, Urban Science, Visual Numerics, Whitecross, WizSoft,
  Xchange

The registration fee includes all conference events, proceedings
and food (breakfast, lunch and breaks.) Come confer with us in
the midst of discussions, demos, food and refreshments. For more
detailed information, please see:

  http://www.acm.org/sigkdd/kdd2000/

messages.subject: [S] Importing from MS Access
messages.body_plain:
We have a table in MS Access, in which a column has many empty cells
(missing values).  When we use the ODBC Connection to import this into SPLUS
(SPLUS 2000),
the file in SPLUS has no missing values or empty cells - SPLUS fills every
empty spot with the corresponding value in the preceding row(s)!  I can see
that there are times when this would be desirable, but to have it happening
by default is very annoying.  To explain it better
   1   A   Fred                      1   A   Fred
   2   B                 becomes:    2   B   Fred
   3   C                             3   C   Fred
   4   D   Jerry                     4   D   Jerry
   5   E   Frank                     4   D   Frank
I know one could solve this by recoding in MS Access, but I would like to
understand why SPLUS does this, seemingly as the default, and what one can
do to switch off this "feature".

Richard Jarrett

messages.subject: [S] Global optimization
messages.body_plain:
I am running S-PLUS 2000 Professional Release 1 on Windows 98.

I am attempting to identify the global optimum of a four-parameter ML
function. The standard libraries for this release of S-PLUS only seem to
offer local optimization routines for multivariate functions (e.g., ms,
nlminb). Are global/robust optimization routines available in S+? I have
tried employing grid searches and Metropolis-type algorithms to obtain
starting values for nlminb, but so far results have been disappointing, in
part because my objective function requires a numerical integration for
evaluation which makes processing quite slow.

Please respond to me directly and I will post a summary of any responses to
the group.

Thank you,

Tyson

************************************************
Tyson Hillard Holmes
PhD Ecology
Ecological Research-Design Consultant
